payloads.title: Oral medicine (MFDS 199702105)
payloads.summary: This medicine is used for seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, chronic idiopathic urticari
payloads.content:

Oral medicine (MFDS 199702105)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199702105. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used for seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, chronic idiopathic urticaria, and pruritus, and for eczema and dermatitis when used together with a topical hydrocortisone preparation.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, chronic idiopathic urticari

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199702105. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults and children aged 6 years and older take 1 tablet (10 mg) once a day before bedtime; patients who are sensitive to adverse reactions take 1/2 tablet (5 mg) each as divided doses in the morning and evening. Adjust the dose appropriately according to age and symptoms. In patients with renal impairment the dosing interval must be adjusted according to the patient's renal function, and in pediatric patients with renal impairment the dose must be adjusted individually taking into account the patient's renal clearance and body weight, so refer to the approved labeling for details.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or to hydroxyzine or piperazine derivatives, patients with renal failure, children under 6 years of age, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, patients with renal impairment (kidney disorder) or hepatic impairment, elderly people, patients with epilepsy and patients at risk of seizures, and patients with predisposing factors for urinary retention (spinal cord lesions, benign prostatic hyperplasia, etc.) should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If any of the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: drowsiness, headache; sometimes malaise, numbness, asthenia, restlessness, abnormal sensation; rarely mild and temporary lethargy, fatigue, dizziness, a heavy feeling in the head, agitation, convulsions, movement disorders, dystonia, fainting, tremor, aggression, confusion, depression, hallucinations, insomnia, tic disorders, memory loss, memory impairment, suicidal thoughts, nightmares; sometimes thirst, dry lips, nausea, loss of appetite, stomach discomfort, indigestion, abdominal pain, stomach pain, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea; rarely vomiting, gastrointestinal disorders, cheilitis, taste disturbance, increased appetite; rarely rapid pulse, arrhythmia, a rise in blood pressure; sometimes palpitations, vasculitis; sometimes decreased white blood cells, decreased neutrophils, increased lymphocytes, increased eosinophils; rarely increased monocytes, increased platelets, decreased platelets, photosensitivity; rarely hypersensitivity and anaphylactic shock; sometimes swelling, itching, rash; rarely hives, angioneurotic edema, fixed drug eruption, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis; rarely blurred vision, conjunctival congestion, disturbance of eye accommodation, oculogyric crisis, vertigo; sometimes liver dysfunction such as elevated AST, ALT, ALP, total bilirubin, GTP, and LDH, jaundice, hepatitis, elevated BUN, glucose in the urine, blood-stained urine; rarely difficulty urinating, bedwetting, urinary retention, joint pain, muscle pain, pharyngitis, cough, nosebleed, bronchospasm, hearing abnormalities, visual abnormalities; sometimes chest pain; rarely irregular menstruation, ringing in the ears, rhinitis, and weight gain.
  • Itching, hives, and similar symptoms may appear after stopping this medicine.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with theophylline, ritonavir, or excessive alcohol while taking it.

This medicine is used to supply vitamin B2 and B6 in physical fatigue, during pregnancy and breast-feeding, and when physical strength is reduced during or after an illness. Through the vitamins and other components it contains, this medicine is used to relieve the symptoms of angular cheilitis, cheilitis, stomatitis, glossitis, eczema and dermatitis. This medicine is used for muscle cramp caused by magnesium deficiency.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to supply vitamin B2 and B6 in physical fatigue, during pregnancy and breast-feeding, and when phy

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202400211. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

People aged 12 years and over and adults take 20 mL per dose, twice a day, between one meal and the next.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by patients with severe renal failure, or by infants under 12 months of age.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the user has or has had hypersensitivity to the caramel component, is a pregnant woman or a woman who may be pregnant or a breast-feeding woman, is a premature baby or a young child, or has hypoproteinemia, cardiac and circulatory dysfunction or renal impairment.
  • If the symptoms do not improve after about 1 month of taking it, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • It may turn the urine yellow and affect clinical test values.
  • Follow the prescribed directions and amounts.

Possible side effects

  • If red spots, diarrhea, asystole and cardiac arrest, or depression of central nervous system function appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • While taking this medicine, do not take phosphates, calcium salts, oral tetracycline preparations, antacids, levodopa or the like.
  • If you take it together with an antialdosterone agent or triamterene, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Avoid tea containing tannin, such as green tea and black tea, while taking it and before and after taking it.

Those aged 12 years and over and adults take 1 to 2 tablets once a day after meals.

payloads.summary: This medicine is used for diarrhea, for the adsorption of gas produced by abnormal fermentation in the digestive tract,
payloads.content:
Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicineThis medicine is used for diarrhea, for the adsorption of gas produced by abnormal fermentation in the digestive tract,

Oral medicine (MFDS 202302823)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202302823. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used for diarrhea, for the adsorption of gas produced by abnormal fermentation in the digestive tract, and as an adsorbent for emergency detoxification in cases of poisoning by medicines and chemicals.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for diarrhea, for the adsorption of gas produced by abnormal fermentation in the digestive tract,

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202302823. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Take 2 to 20 g of medicinal charcoal in 1 day, divided into several doses. In acute poisoning, administer medicinal charcoal within 30 minutes after ingestion of the poisonous substance. When the amount of poisonous substance ingested is known, the recommended dose of medicinal charcoal is usually 5-10 times the amount of the ingested poisonous substance. Increase or decrease the amount appropriately according to age and symptoms as directed by a doctor.

Warning

  • Since this medicine impairs the imaging of esophageal erosion, do not take it if a corrosive substance has been ingested.
  • Do not use this medicine in patients with diabetes without a doctor's diagnosis and prescription.

Precautions for use

  • When this medicine is used as an antidote for oral poisoning, giving medicinal charcoal together with ipecac syrup is not recommended, because the ipecac syrup is adsorbed by the medicinal charcoal and vomiting is thereby prevented.
  • If ipecac syrup and medicinal charcoal are used together, it is recommended that the medicinal charcoal be given after vomiting has been induced and completed.
  • This medicine should be given after gastric aspiration or gastric lavage has been completed with the involvement of a doctor.
  • Within 2 hours of giving medicinal charcoal, the charcoal adsorbs other medicines and therefore reduces their effect.
  • This medicine may colour the stool black.

Possible side effects

  • Indigestion may occur.

Interactions

  • Ice cream and sherbet lower the adsorptive power of medicinal charcoal, so do not take them together with this medicine.

This medicine is used for the temporary relief of itchy eyes, watery eyes, runny nose, itching of the nose or throat, sneezing, nasal congestion, and sinus congestion.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for the temporary relief of itchy eyes, watery eyes, runny nose, itching of the nose or throat, sn

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202002848. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 12 years and over and adults take 4 packets (20 mL) at a time, those aged 6 years and over but under 12 years take 2 packets (10 mL) at a time, and those aged 2 years and over but under 6 years take 1 packet (5 mL) at a time, every 4 to 6 hours, and do not exceed 4 doses in 24 hours.

Warning

  • If a severe skin adverse reaction such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis occurs while taking a medicine containing pseudoephedrine, stop taking it and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants under 2 years of age and patients with heart disease, high blood pressure, thyroid disease, diabetes, glaucoma, or a respiratory disorder such as asthma or chronic bronchitis should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it for about 1 week, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If anxiety, dizziness, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, erythema, numerous small pustules, or insomnia occurs, if a sore throat lasts 2 days or longer, or if headache, fever, rash, nausea, vomiting, or ischemic colitis (sudden abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, etc.) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If symptoms of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (sudden severe headache, thunderclap headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures, visual disturbances, etc.) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Excitement (especially in children) and drowsiness may occur.

Interactions

  • Do not take together with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs - some medicines for depression, mental and emotional disorders, and Parkinson's disease).
  • People who stopped taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (some medicines for depression, mental and emotional disorders, and Parkinson's disease) within the past 2 weeks should not take this medicine.

Those aged 15 years and older take 3 sachets at a time; those aged 11 years and older but under 15 years take 2 sachets at a time; those aged 7 years and older but under 11 years take 1½ sachets at a time; those aged 3 years and older but under 7 years take 1 sachet at a time; and those aged 2 years and older but under 3 years take 3/4 sachet at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals and, if necessary, at bedtime, leaving an interval of 4 hours between doses.

Children aged 12 years and over and adults take 1 to 3 sachets a day in divided doses, and the dose may be adjusted according to individual response. Dissolve 1 sachet in 125 mL of water and take it.   • If edema (swelling), shortness of breath, fatigue, symptoms of dehydration, heart failure or the like occurs, stop taking the medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, ten

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202402681. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, adults take 1 to 2 packets (250 to 500 mg) per dose, 2 times a day every 12 hours. For acute gout, adults take 3 packets (750 mg) as the first dose and then 1 packet (250 mg) every 8 hours until the attack subsides. For skeletal muscle disorders, pain after surgery, pain after tooth extraction, dysmenorrhea, tendinitis (inflammation of the tendon), and bursitis, adults take 2 packets (500 mg) as the first dose and then 1 packet (250 mg) every 6 to 8 hours. Do not exceed a total daily dose of 5 packets (1,250 mg). For migraine, adults take 3 packets (750 mg) as the first dose. If necessary, an additional 1 to 2 packets (250 to 500 mg) may be taken a day, taken 30 minutes after the first dose. Do not exceed a total daily dose of 5 packets (1,250 mg). Increase or decrease the dose as appropriate according to age and symptoms. Shake the suspension well to mix it before use, then take it.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood disorders, liver disorder, cardiac insufficiency, kidney disorder or high blood pressure, patients with hypersensitivity to the ingredients of this medicine or to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as aspirin, those who have experienced asthma, rhinitis, nasal polyps, urticaria or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, and pregnant women (in late pregnancy) must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer or blood disorders or those who have experienced them, patients with a tendency to bleed, patients with liver disorder or a history of it, patients with kidney disorder or a history of it and patients with reduced renal blood flow, patients with impaired cardiac function, patients with high blood pressure, those who have experienced hypersensitivity, patients with bronchial asthma, patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and patients with mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), and elderly people should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If any of the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rarely, shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, bradycardia (slow pulse), cold sweat, swelling, etc.), PIE syndrome (pulmonary infiltration with eosinophilia: accompanied by fever, wheezing, cough and sputum), hives; sometimes rash, itching; rarely hematemesis (vomiting of blood), gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation; sometimes stomach discomfort, stomach pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, indigestion, heartburn, diarrhea, constipation, stomatitis (inflammation of the mouth); rarely abdominal bloating, black stools, thirst; rarely blood disorders such as agranulocytosis, eosinophilia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia (destruction of red blood cells), reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time); rarely elevated GOT and GPT values, jaundice, hepatitis; rarely renal impairment (kidney disorder), glomerulonephritis (kidney inflammation), blood in the urine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis (kidney inflammation), nephrotic syndrome, renal (kidney) papillary necrosis, protein in the urine, renal failure; rarely aseptic meningitis, severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever or disturbance of consciousness; sometimes drowsiness, impaired cognitive function; rarely dizziness, headache, numbness of the hands and feet, decreased vitality, fatigue, depression, abnormal dreams, loss of concentration, disorientation (impaired orientation), insomnia, muscle pain, muscle weakness; sometimes eczema, sweating, purpura; rarely photosensitivity, hair loss, redness (congested and reddened), necrolysis, erythema multiforme (red spots), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (skin-mucosa-eye syndrome), hives, epidermolysis bullosa, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, fixed drug eruption, ringing in the ears, hearing impairment, visual impairment; sometimes swelling, difficulty breathing; rarely palpitations (pounding heart), myasthenia (muscle weakness), congestive heart failure, eosinophilic pneumonia, anaphylactoid reactions, menstrual disorders, chills (feeling cold and shivering) and fever, vasculitis (inflammation of the blood vessels), high blood sugar, or low blood sugar.

Interactions

  • Do not take together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (NSAIDs) or naproxen derivatives.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with hydantoin antiepileptics, sulfonamides, sulfonylurea hypoglycemic agents, propranolol and other blockers, ACE inhibitors, loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics, probenecid, aspirin, lithium, methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), zidovudine, or new quinolone antibiotics (such as enoxacin).

Adults and children aged 8 years and over take 20 to 40 mL (1 to 2 sachets) a day, based on a package unit of 1 sachet (20 mL). Depending on the symptoms, children in particular may take 20 mL (1 sachet) every two days. Dissolve 20 mL (1 sachet) of this medicine in water to make 50 mL and take it. It is recommended to take it in the morning. Children from 6 months to 7 years of age, based on a package unit of 1 sachet (8 mL), take 8 mL (1 sachet) a day at 6 months to 1 year of age, 8 to 16 mL (1 to 2 sachets) a day at 1 to 4 years of age, and 16 to 32 mL (2 to 4 sachets) a day at 4 to 7 years of age. When 1 sachet (8 mL) a day is taken, take it in the morning, and when more than 1 sachet (8 mL) a day is taken, divide it between morning and evening. Dissolve 8 mL (1 sachet) of this medicine in water to make 50 mL and take it.

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by patients with inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, etc.) or toxic megacolon, by patients with intestinal perforation or at risk of intestinal perforation, by patients who have or are suspected of having intestinal obstruction, by patients with intestinal stricture, or by patients with abdominal pain of unknown cause.

  • In children, do not give this medicine for 3 months or more, and do not give this medicine for a long period without the judgment of a doctor.

  • In adults, if abdominal pain and abdominal distension, diarrhea or nausea appears, if vomiting, urgent defecation or fecal incontinence uncommonly appears, if electrolyte disturbance (hyponatremia, hypokalemia, etc.), dehydration or erythema appears at an unknown frequency, or if a hypersensitivity reaction (itching, rash, facial edema, angioedema, urticaria, anaphylactic shock, etc.) very rarely appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

However, take it after each meal and, if necessary, at bedtime, and as a rule leave an interval of 4 hours between doses.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, people who have had asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, infants under 3 months of age, and people who are taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) or who stopped taking them within the past 2 weeks must not take this medicine.

  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

Adults and children aged 12 years and older take 4 tablets every 8 hours. Do not exceed 12 tablets within 24 hours.

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer or severe blood disorders, patients with severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder or severely reduced cardiac function, patients with aspirin-induced asthma (asthma attacks triggered by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents) or a history of it, people who have taken barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants or alcohol, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.

  • If shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, reddening of the whole body, angioedema, urticaria, an asthma attack, etc.), thrombocytopenia, granulocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, methemoglobinemia, decreased platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), cyanosis, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation (a hole forming), hypersensitivity symptoms (facial swelling, sweating, low blood pressure), rash, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), abnormal liver function such as elevated AST and elevated ALT, or fixed drug eruption occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take it together with other anti-inflammatory analgesics, other products containing acetaminophen, barbiturates, or tricyclic antidepressants.

Those 15 years and older take 3 sachets at a time, those 11 years and older but under 15 years take 2 sachets at a time, those 7 years and older but under 11 years take 3/2 sachet at a time, those 3 years and older but under 7 years take 1 sachet at a time, and those 2 years and older but under 3 years take 3/4 sachet at a time, 3 times a day, avoiding an empty stomach.   • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine and those who have experienced it, people who have had asthma when taking this medicine or its ingredients, other antipyretic analgesics, or cold remedies, infants under 3 months of age, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.

  • Do not take this medicine together with other antipyretic analgesics, cold medicines or sedatives.

payloads.content:

Oral medicine (MFDS 201310592)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201310592. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used to inhibit thrombus formation in myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction, and unstable angina, to inhibit thrombus formation after coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) or percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty (PTCA), and to reduce cardiovascular risk in high-risk patients (patients with multiple risk factors such as a family history of ischemic heart disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, obesity, and diabetes).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to inhibit thrombus formation in myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction, and unstable angina,

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201310592. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults take 1 tablet as 1 dose, 1 time a day. Since this medicine is an enteric-coated tablet, it may be taken before meals with plenty of water.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or to other salicylate preparations, analgesics, anti-inflammatory agents or antirheumatic agents, patients with peptic ulcer or aspirin-induced asthma or a history of it, patients with hemophilia, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency or a tendency to bleed, patients receiving concomitant methotrexate at doses of 15 mg or more per week (15 mg/week), and pregnant women in the third trimester must not take this medicine.
  • Do not take this medicine during the first and second trimesters of pregnancy unless it is absolutely necessary.
  • Before using this medicine, patients with kidney disorder, cardiovascular circulatory dysfunction (renal vascular disease, congestive heart failure, fluid depletion, major surgery, sepsis or major bleeding events, etc.), liver disorder, impaired cardiac function or bronchial asthma, patients before surgery, young children aged 3 years or under, elderly people, patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, patients with Reye's syndrome, patients aged 14 years or under with chickenpox or influenza infection, and patients with gout should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Because there is a risk of bleeding, tell your doctor that you are taking this medicine if you are going to have surgery (including dental surgery).
  • Take care not to damage the enteric coating of this medicine.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms (e.g., difficulty breathing, generalized flushing, angioedema, urticaria), asthma attacks, hypersensitivity (erythema, itching, nasal congestion, cardiac and respiratory disorders, occasionally rash, edema, urticaria, rhinitis-like symptoms, conjunctivitis), rarely toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), exfoliative dermatitis, aplastic anemia, anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), ringing in the ears, deafness, dizziness, headache, agitation, liver disorder, very rarely transient liver damage, kidney disorder, acute renal failure, hyperventilation, metabolic acidosis, excessive lowering of body temperature, collapse, or coldness of the limbs occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Loss of appetite, heartburn, stomach pain, nausea, and vomiting may occur.

Interactions

  • Other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics and salicylate preparations, and methotrexate at doses of 15 mg or more per week (15 mg/week), must not be used together with this medicine, because concomitant use may increase bleeding or reduce kidney function.
  • People taking anticoagulants, some non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as ibuprofen and naproxen, thrombolytics, other platelet aggregation inhibitors, hemostatics, antidiabetic agents (insulin preparations, tolbutamide, etc.), uricosuric agents (benzbromarone, probenecid), thiazide diuretics, lithium preparations, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, digoxin, systemically acting adrenocortical hormone preparations (excluding hydrocortisone used as replacement therapy for Addison's disease), angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, or valproic acid preparations should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not mix this medicine with alkaline preparations (for example, sodium bicarbonate, magnesium carbonate) or with preparations that easily absorb moisture.
  • Concomitant use with alcohol increases damage to the gastrointestinal mucosa, and the synergistic effect of this medicine and alcohol may prolong bleeding time.

Adults aged 15 years and older take 1 bottle 3 times a day; those aged 11 years and older but under 15 years take 2/3 bottle 3 times a day; those aged 7 years and older but under 11 years take 1/2 bottle 3 times a day; those aged 3 years and older but under 7 years take 1/3 bottle 3 times a day; and those aged 1 year and older but under 3 years take 1/4 bottle 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.If necessary, take it at bedtime, and as a rule leave an interval of 4 hours between doses.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.It may cause liver damage.Very rarely, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of hypersensitivity appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).It may cause liver damage.Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.This medicine contains aspartame, which is metabolized to phenylalanine in the body, so patients with phenylketonuria who need to restrict their phenylalanine intake must not take it.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or a history of it, people who have had asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, and infants under 3 months of age must not take this medicine.

  • Follow the specified dosage and administration carefully.
  • When it is given to children, give it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, light-headedness, or, rarely, shock (urticaria, swelling, chest tightness, etc. together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweats, and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), asthma, listlessness of the whole body, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes turning yellow), interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, and fever), pseudoaldosteronism (decreased urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, a rise in blood pressure or headache, etc.), or myopathy (weakness, cramps in the limbs, paralysis, etc.) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

How to take it

Adults aged 15 years and older take 1 sachet (100 ml) at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. If necessary, take it at bedtime, and allow 4 hours between doses.

  • Very rarely, in patients taking acetaminophen, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported, and if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, dizziness, anxiety, tremor or insomnia appears, or if shock rarely appears (urticaria, swelling and a feeling of tightness in the chest right after taking it, together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat and difficulty breathing), or if mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), asthma, hepatic impairment (generalized languor, jaundice, etc.), interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.), pseudoaldosteronism (reduced urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heavy eyelids, stiffening of the hands, a rise in blood pressure or headache, etc.) or myopathy (languor, cramp of the limbs, paralysis, etc.) appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, antiparkinson drugs, etc.), antitussives and expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral medicines for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, allergy medicines).

How it works

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 200511037. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults and elderly people (the aged), when they feel an urge to smoke, place 1 tablet of this medicine in the mouth and take it by sucking it slowly without chewing or swallowing it. At first, take 1 tablet of this medicine every 1 to 2 hours. Usually 8 to 12 tablets a day are taken, and do not exceed a maximum of 25 tablets a day. Take this medicine in the following order. Place 1 tablet of this medicine in the mouth and suck it until a strong taste is felt. Then place it between the gum and the cheek, and when the taste fades, repeat in the same way, sucking until it dissolves completely. The treatment period is at least 3 months; from 3 months onward the dose should be reduced in stages, and treatment should be stopped when the dose of this medicine has been reduced to 1 to 2 tablets a day. In general, nicotine replacement products such as this medicine are not recommended for use for more than 6 months.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with unstable angina or worsening angina, patients who have had a myocardial infarction within the last 3 months, patients in the late acute infarction period, patients with clinically relevant cardiac arrhythmias including severe cardiac arrhythmias, patients with severe cardiovascular disease such as systemic hypertension or peripheral vascular disease, patients with acute stroke or recent cerebrovascular disease, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, children and adolescents under 18 years of age, and non-smokers and occasional smokers must not use this medicine.
  • Before using this medicine, patients with cardiovascular disease such as active esophagitis, oral (inside the mouth) and pharyngeal inflammation, gastritis, peptic ulcer, occlusive (closed and blocked) arterial disease, stable angina, heart failure, decompensated heart failure, myocardial infarction, cardiac arrhythmia, vasospasm, uncontrolled high blood pressure, or arterial bypass grafting or angioplasty, elderly people, patients with renal or hepatic failure, patients with diabetes, hyperthyroidism, or pheochromocytoma, and people receiving anticonvulsant treatment or with a history of epilepsy should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If insomnia, dizziness, headache, tremor, nausea, vomiting, indigestion, upper abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal distension, hiccups, gastritis, dry mouth, stomatitis, esophagitis, oral discomfort, difficulty swallowing, belching, excessive salivation, pharyngitis, cough, sore throat, difficulty breathing, palpitations, atrial arrhythmia, tachycardia (rapid pulse), hypersensitivity, angioneurotic edema, urticaria, ulcerative stomatitis, anaphylaxis, asthenia, fatigue, malaise, or influenza-like illness occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.Occasionally, mild throat irritation, increased salivation, hiccups, indigestion, or heartburn may occur at the beginning of treatment.

Interactions

  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you use it together with paracetamol, caffeine, imipramine, oxazepam, pentazocine, propranolol, theophylline, warfarin, estrogen, lignocaine, phenacetin, insulin, adrenergic antagonists (prazosin, labetalol, etc.), flecainide, adrenergic agonists (isoprenaline, phenylephrine), propoxyphene, furosemide diuretics, H2 antagonists, beta blockers, theophylline, tacrine, clozapine, or ropinirole.

Why this one

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Children aged 6 months and over take 0.4 to 0.6 mL per kg of body weight per dose, at intervals of 4 to 6 hours when needed, and must not exceed 4 doses a day (28 mg/kg). For children weighing 30 kg or less, do not exceed 25 mL a day. When the body weight is known it is more appropriate to use the amount based on body weight, so refer to the approved product information for details.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormality, liver impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, high blood pressure or bronchial asthma or by those who have had them, by people who have had asthma, urticaria or an allergy in response to aspirin or another non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesic, by patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, or by a pregnant woman or a woman who may be pregnant or a breast-feeding woman.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the user has or has had peptic ulcer, blood abnormality, a bleeding tendency, liver impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, high blood pressure or hypersensitivity, is a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, is elderly or a child, has stomach cancer, or is taking low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke, especially a patient with an autoimmune disease (SLE, MCTD).

Possible side effects

  • If any of the following appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rarely shock (chest discomfort, chills, difficulty breathing, fall in blood pressure, etc.); blood disorders such as aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time) and eosinophilia; peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, or very rarely dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal distension and constipation; Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome) or toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome); drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency; acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis; jaundice and increases in GOT, GPT and AL-P; induction of an asthma attack; urticaria, eczema, purpura, occasionally rash and itching; rarely visual disturbance such as blurred or dim vision, hearing loss, tinnitus and abnormal taste; aseptic meningitis, severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever or disturbance of consciousness; fall in blood pressure, rise in blood pressure and palpitations; acute renal failure, oliguria and hematuria together with proteinuria and increases in BUN and blood creatinine; hyperkalemia, reduced urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath and languor; acute pulmonary edema; occasionally periorbital edema; and very rarely malaise, fever and nosebleed.

Interactions

  • Do not use it together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when using it together with glucocorticoids, alcohol, digoxin, phenytoin, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, sulfonylureas, diuretics, antihypertensive medicines, ACE inhibitors, furosemide, aspirin, lithium, methotrexate, or coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin).

Those 15 years and older take 1 sachet (5 g) at a time, those 11 years and older but under 15 years take 2/3 sachet at a time, and those 7 years and older but under 11 years take 1/2 sachet at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals, dissolved in water.   • When it is given to children, give it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.

  • If rash, redness, itching, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), light-headedness, high anion gap metabolic acidosis, or, rarely, shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling, chest tightness, etc. immediately after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweats, and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, in which rash and redness and blisters like burns appear on the skin of the whole body or on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes), asthma, listlessness of the whole body, jaundice, or interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, and fever) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussive expectorants, other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).

Those aged 15 years and older take 15 mL per dose, those aged 11 years to under 15 years take 10 mL, those aged 7 years to under 11 years take 7.5 mL, those aged 3 years to under 7 years take 5 mL, and those aged 2 years to under 3 years take 3.75 mL, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals and, if necessary, at bedtime. How to use it in the mouth

Use 15 mL per dose, twice a day: rinse the mouth or gargle for about 1 minute and then spit it out; use it after brushing the teeth. In the case of stomatitis caused by dentures, soak and clean the dentures for 15 minutes twice a day. The amount may be increased or decreased appropriately according to age and symptoms.

  • Temporary parotitis, an increase in staining on the teeth or the surface of the mouth (the inside of the mouth), an increase in the formation of supragingival calculus, a change in the sense of taste and the like may occur.

  • Do not take together with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs - some medicines for depression, mental and emotional disorders, and Parkinson's disease).

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, fever and pain due to a cold, low back pain, dysmenorrhea, postoperative pain and ankylosing spondylitis, headache, toothache, muscle pain, neuralgia, acute gout, psoriatic arthritis, soft tissue injuries (sprains, contusions), and non-articular rheumatic diseases (tendinitis, tenosynovitis, bursitis).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, fever and pain due to a c

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 198601920. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200-600 mg at a time, 3-4 times a day. Up to a maximum of 3,200 mg a day may be administered. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30-40 mg per kg of body weight at a time, 3 to 4 times a day. For mild to moderate pain and colds, adults take 200-400 mg at a time, 3 to 4 times a day. The dose may be increased or decreased as appropriate according to age and symptoms. In children, those aged 11 to 14 years take 200-250 mg (10 to 12.5 ml), those aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg (7.5 to 10 ml), those aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg (5 to 7.5 ml), and those aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg (2.5 to 5 ml) at a time, 3 to 4 times a day.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, gastrointestinal ulcers, gastrointestinal bleeding or a history of it, severe blood abnormalities, liver disorder, kidney disorder, cardiac insufficiency, high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma or a history of it, people who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions to aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors), patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery (heart artery) bypass surgery (CABG), pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as chemotherapy, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with blood abnormalities or a history of them, a bleeding tendency, cirrhosis, liver disorder or a history of it, kidney disorder or a history of it, cardiac insufficiency or heart disease, high blood pressure, or a history of hypersensitivity, patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and patients with mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), patients with ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, or chickenpox, elderly people, children under 2 years of age, pregnant women, and breastfeeding women should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the specified dosage and administration carefully.
  • Take care when driving or operating machinery after taking it.
  • Without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist, do not take it for pain for more than 10 days (adults) or more than 5 days (children), and do not take it for fever for more than 3 days.

Possible side effects

  • If the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, etc.); blood disorders such as decreased hematocrit and hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, decreased granulocytes, white blood cells, and platelets, reduced platelet function, and increased eosinophils; peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation (a hole), ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, vomiting of blood, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, thirst, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, mouth ulcers, constipation, black stools; Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), photosensitivity reactions of unknown frequency, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis; hepatitis, jaundice, elevated GOT, GPT, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP), liver disorder; hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reactions, asthma attacks, urticaria, eczema, purple spots, rash, itching, asthma, bronchoconstriction, difficulty breathing or wheezing; visual disturbances such as scotoma; hearing loss (deafness), tinnitus (ringing in the ears), taste disturbance, vertigo, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness, aseptic meningitis or meningitis; drop in blood pressure, rise in blood pressure, palpitations, heart failure, myocardial infarction or angina, Kounis syndrome; acute renal failure, oliguria (decreased urination), hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis (kidney inflammation), nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath, lethargy, periorbital edema (swelling around the eyes), facial edema (facial swelling), malaise, fever, nosebleed, edema, peripheral edema, and Kounis syndrome of unknown frequency.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, alcohol or high-dose methotrexate.
  • If you take it together with ACE inhibitors, lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin, etc.), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or the like, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Those aged 11 years and over and adults take 1 capsule at a time, 1 to 3 times a day, avoiding an empty stomach. Leave an interval of at least 4 hours between doses.

  • While taking this medicine, do not take other antipyretic analgesics, cold medicines, or sedatives.
  • Before taking this medicine, people who are given other medicines such as diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, or steroids and people who take low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

This medicine is used for diarrhea, for the adsorption of gas produced by abnormal fermentation in the digestive tract, and as an adsorbent for emergency detoxification in poisoning by drugs and chemicals. (However, medicinal charcoal does not adsorb cyanide, and it is relatively ineffective at adsorbing alcohol, aliphatic hydrocarbons, lithium salts, corrosive sodium chloride, heavy metals such as iron, lead, and lead cyanide, boric acid, other inorganic acids, and petroleum distillates.)

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for diarrhea, for the adsorption of gas produced by abnormal fermentation in the digestive tract,

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202302822. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Take 2 to 20 g of medicinal charcoal a day, divided into several doses. In acute poisoning, medicinal charcoal is administered within 30 minutes after ingestion of the poisonous substance. (When the amount of the ingested poisonous substance is known, the recommended dose of medicinal charcoal is usually 5-10 times the amount of the ingested poisonous substance.)
Increase or decrease the dose appropriately according to age and symptoms, following the instructions of a doctor.

Warning

  • Because it degrades the imaging of esophageal erosion, do not use it when a corrosive substance has been ingested.
  • Do not use it in patients with diabetes without a doctor's diagnosis and prescription.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine should be administered after gastric aspiration or gastric lavage has been completed with the involvement of a doctor.
  • Within 2 hours of administering medicinal charcoal, the charcoal adsorbs other medicines and so reduces their effect.
  • This medicine may turn the stools black.

Possible side effects

  • Be careful, as indigestion may occur and as the adsorption of vitamins, minerals and the like may cause nutritional disturbance.

Interactions

  • Ice cream and sherbet lower the adsorptive power of medicinal charcoal, so do not take them together with it.
  • When it is used as an antidote for oral poisoning, do not take it together with ipecac syrup.
  • The ipecac syrup may be adsorbed by the medicinal charcoal and so prevent vomiting.
  • If ipecac syrup and medicinal charcoal are used at the same time, it is recommended that the medicinal charcoal be given after vomiting has been induced and has finished.

If necessary it may be taken at bedtime, and in principle the interval between doses should be 4 hours.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine or those who have experienced it, people who have had an asthma attack when taking this medicine or its ingredients, other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, and infants under 3 months of age and children under 2 years of age must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, the following should consult a doctor or pharmacist: infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza; children under 2 years of age when it is absolutely necessary; people with a constitution prone to urticaria, contact dermatitis, bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis, migraine or food allergy; patients who have had allergic symptoms caused by a medicine; people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, edema, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma or difficulty urinating; the elderly; people with a weak body or a high fever; people with persistent or recurrent stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems; pregnant women or women who may be pregnant; breastfeeding women; and people with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough with excessive phlegm, a cough lasting or recurring for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash or persistent headache.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • When giving it to a child, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, rarely shock (urticaria, swelling, or chest tightness immediately after taking it, together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, difficulty breathing, etc.), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome: accompanied by high fever, with severe symptoms such as rash and redness and burn-like blistering), asthma, liver function disorder (generalized lassitude, jaundice), interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.), pseudoaldosteronism (decreased urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, raised blood pressure, headache, etc.), or myopathy (weakness, cramps in the limbs, paralysis) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussives and expectorants, other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • People who are within 2 weeks of stopping MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) must not take this medicine.
  • If it is taken together with diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol, potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, etacrynic acid), or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide), consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.

Those aged 15 years and over take 1 sachet (20 mL), those aged 11 years and over but under 15 years take 2/3 of a sachet, those aged 7 years and over but under 11 years take 1/2 of a sachet, those aged 3 years and over but under 7 years take 1/3 of a sachet, and those aged 2 years and over but under 3 years take 1/4 of a sachet, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take this medicine together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • People with or with a history of hypersensitivity to this medicine, people who have had asthma after taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants (newborns) under 3 months of age, and people who are taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) or who are within 2 weeks of stopping them must not take this medicine.

  • If symptoms do not improve after taking it 5 to 6 times, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.
  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • When administering it to children, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.

  • If rash and redness (congested and reddened skin), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema (swelling), difficulty urinating, persistent or severe thirst, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, shock symptoms (urticaria, edema and chest tightness immediately after taking the medicine, together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat and difficulty breathing), Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome: severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash and redness and blistering like a burn), asthma, generalized listlessness, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes turning yellow), or interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, breathlessness, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussive-expectorants (cough and phlegm remedies), other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis [nasal inflammation], motion sickness remedies, anti-allergy remedies).

How it works

This medicine is used for difficulty in expectorating sputum in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pu

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 198600267. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

This medicine may be diluted to a lower concentration with sodium chloride solution for injection, sodium chloride solution for inhalation, sterile distilled water for injection or sterile distilled water for inhalation. For nebulization therapy using a face mask, a mouthpiece or a tracheostomy, nebulize 1 to 10 mL every 2 to 6 hours. The recommended amount is 3 to 5 mL nebulized 3 to 4 times a day. Nebulization therapy using a nebulization tent or an inhaler (Croupette) is a method needed in special cases, and it is used individually according to the personal needs of the patient and the convenience of the method of administration. This method of administration requires a large volume of solution, and sometimes as much as about 300 mL may be required for a single treatment. The recommended amount should be an amount that can maintain a very dense mist-like state inside the tent or the inhaler during the treatment period. Intermittent or continuous administration over a long period is preferable. For direct instillation, give 1 to 2 mL every hour. For the regular treatment of a patient who has had a tracheostomy, give 1 to 2 mL through the tracheostomy every 1 to 4 hours. When a small plastic catheter is inserted into the trachea under local anesthesia through a direct incision to give it directly to a specific part of the bronchial tree, give 2 to 5 mL every 1 to 4 hours using a syringe connected to the catheter. When it is given using a percutaneous intrabronchial catheter, give 1 to 2 mL of this medicine every 1 to 4 hours with a syringe connected to the catheter. For diagnostic bronchography, give 1 to 2 mL 2 to 3 times by nebulization or by intrabronchial instillation before the bronchography is performed.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine must not use this medicine.
  • Before using this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the user has bronchial asthma or accompanying respiratory insufficiency, is a pregnant woman or a woman who may be pregnant or a breast-feeding woman, is a child, or is elderly.
  • Do not use it as an injection or as eye drops.
  • After nebulization therapy the face mask may stick to the face, but it comes off easily when washed with water.

Possible side effects

  • If bronchial obstruction, bronchospasm, rash or difficulty breathing occasionally appears, or if anaphylaxis rarely appears, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • A slight odor (smell of sulfur) may appear, nausea, vomiting and loss of appetite may occasionally appear, and bloody sputum, chills, fever, runny nose, stomatitis, drowsiness, a feeling of pressure in the chest and irritation of the trachea and bronchi may rarely appear.

Interactions

  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when it is used together with an antibiotic, tetracycline, erythromycin, bromhexine or the like.

For mild to moderate pain and colds, take 200-400 mg at a time, 3-4 times a day. Children take the following single dose 3-4 times a day; for children weighing less than 30 kg the daily amount must not exceed 500 mg (25 ml), and it is preferable not to take it on an empty stomach. Children 11-14 years of age are recommended to take 200-250 mg (10-13 ml) at a time, children 7-10 years of age 150-200 mg (8-10 ml) at a time, children 3-6 years of age 100-150 mg (5-8 ml) at a time, and children 1-2 years of age 50-100 mg (3-5 ml) at a time. Increase or decrease the dose appropriately according to age and symptoms.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.

  • When non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics including this medicine are taken, serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke that may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation, may appear.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, patients with or a history of gastrointestinal ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding, patients with severe blood disorders, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma or a history of it, patients with or a history of hypersensitivity reactions such as asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions to aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors), patients in whom pain occurs before or after coronary artery (heart artery) bypass graft surgery (CABG), pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy, and patients with genetic problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with or a history of blood disorders, patients with a bleeding tendency, patients with cirrhosis or with or a history of liver disorder, patients with or a history of kidney disorder, patients with cardiac insufficiency, heart disease, high blood pressure, hypersensitivity, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people, children, pregnant women, nursing mothers, and those who have experienced hypersensitivity or allergy to Yellow No. 5 (Sunset Yellow FCF) should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not take more than the recommended dose.
  • In case of an overdose, get prompt medical treatment even if there are no obvious symptoms or signs.

Possible side effects

  • If any of the following appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: shock, anaphylactoid reaction, chest discomfort (heartburn), chills, difficulty breathing, fall in blood pressure; decreased hematocrit, decreased hemoglobin, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), eosinophilia; peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, hematemesis, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, thirst, stomatitis, abdominal distension, oral ulcer, constipation, black stools; mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), photosensitivity reaction (unknown frequency), drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash; hepatitis, jaundice, hepatic dysfunction such as increases in GOT, GPT and alkaline phosphatase (ALP), liver impairment; hypersensitivity, anaphylactic reaction, asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purpura (purple spots), rash, itching, asthma, bronchoconstriction, difficulty breathing, wheezing; visual disturbance such as scotoma (a blind area of the visual field), hearing loss, tinnitus, abnormal taste, vertigo, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness; aseptic meningitis or meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever or disturbance of consciousness, etc.); fall in blood pressure, rise in blood pressure, palpitations, heart failure, myocardial infarction or angina; acute renal failure, oliguria (decreased urine), hematuria, proteinuria, increases in BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, reduced urine volume, generalized edema, shortness of breath, languor, periorbital edema, facial edema, malaise, fever, nosebleed, edema, peripheral edema, metabolic acidosis, loss of consciousness and convulsion.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (NSAIDs).
  • People who are taking low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking it together with ACE inhibitors, lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs).
  • Do not breast-feed while taking this medicine.

Children aged 12 years or under take the recommended amount as 1 dose every 4-6 hours as needed. Take the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible period, and do not take more than 5 doses (75 mg/kg) in 1 day. For the recommended dose by age group, refer to the approved product information.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other anti-inflammatory analgesics.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients who take warfarin long-term or who have taken lithium or thiazide diuretics should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Oral medicine (MFDS 201701325)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201701325. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used to relieve nasal congestion, runny nose, sneezing, watery eyes, throat pain and a feeling of heaviness in the head caused by a head cold (acute rhinitis), allergic rhinitis or sinusitis.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to relieve nasal congestion, runny nose, sneezing, watery eyes, throat pain and a feeling of heavi

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201701325. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

People aged 15 years and over and adults take 1 film per dose, 3 times a day, letting it dissolve in the mouth. The interval between doses must be 4 hours or more. Take this medicine (film) in the following order. Open the aluminum sheet, peel it away slowly from the mouth and take out only the medicine (film). (Do not swallow the whole aluminum sheet. It may lead to an unexpected accident such as the sheet lodging in the mucous membrane of the esophagus.) Place this medicine (film) on the tongue and take it while it dissolves in the saliva. This medicine (film) is a film that dissolves easily in water, so do not handle it with wet hands. This medicine (film) dissolves in the mouth immediately, but if it sticks to the throat, drink water and swallow it. Also, if there is little saliva and it is difficult to take, put water in the mouth and take it while it dissolves.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by children under 15 years of age, or by people who are taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian medicines, etc.) or stopped taking them less than 2 weeks ago.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the user is a pregnant woman or a woman who may be pregnant, is elderly, has a high fever, difficulty urinating, dry mouth, glaucoma, diabetes, thyroid dysfunction, a heart disease or high blood pressure, smokes, has asthma, chronic bronchitis or emphysema, or has a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough that lasts for 1 week or more or recurs, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash or persistent headache.
  • Follow the prescribed directions and amounts.
  • When it is given to a child, give it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • If the symptoms do not improve after 5 to 6 days of taking it, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Because drowsiness may appear after taking it, take care when driving or operating machinery.

Possible side effects

  • If rash, redness, itching, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, dizziness, insomnia, nervousness, headache, convulsion, difficulty urinating, facial flushing, photophobia, symptoms of aplastic anemia (blue bruises, nosebleed, gum bleeding, fever, pale skin and mucous membranes, fatigue, palpitations, difficulty breathing, dizziness, hematuria) or agranulocytosis (high fever, chills, sore throat, etc.) appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, antiparkinson drugs, etc.), other oral medicines for rhinitis, oral medicines containing antihistamines (cold remedies, antitussives and expectorants, motion sickness medicines, allergy medicines, etc.), or gastrointestinal analgesic and antispasmodic medicines.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.

This medicine is used for chronic constipation, constipation in infants, young children, and children, and constipation after childbirth.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for chronic constipation, constipation in infants, young children, and children, and constipation

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201907041. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For chronic constipation, adults take 15 to 30 mL a day before breakfast for the first 2 to 3 days, and thereafter continue with 10 to 15 mL a day. In severe cases up to 45 mL may be taken. Children (7 to 14 years) take 15 mL a day for the first 2 to 3 days and thereafter continue with 10 mL a day. Young children (1 to 6 years) take 5 to 10 mL a day, and infants (under 12 months) take 5 mL a day.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease), gastrointestinal obstruction, abdominal pain of unknown cause, a low-galactose diet (galactosemia), or gastrointestinal perforation or a risk of it, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, infants, young children and children, the elderly, and patients with diabetes, fructose intolerance, fluid and electrolyte imbalance, acute gastritis or chronic constipation should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If loose stools or diarrhea occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Belching, cramping abdominal discomfort, and occasionally borborygmi, abdominal bloating, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea, and vomiting may occur.

Interactions

  • Patients who take α-glucosidase inhibitors such as acarbose, broad-spectrum antibiotics, diuretics, corticosteroids, amphotericin B, cardiac glycosides, or antacids should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
