This medicine is used for disinfection of lacerations, burns and wounds, disinfection of ulcers and abscesses, disinfection of infected skin surfaces, disinfection of surgical sites, and disinfection of injection and catheter sites.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Topical medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for disinfection of lacerations, burns and wounds, disinfection of ulcers and abscesses, disinfect

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 200901683. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

Apply an appropriate amount to the affected area several times in 1 day.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, newborns and infants under 6 months of age, patients with thyroid dysfunction (especially nodular goiter, endemic goiter, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, etc.), renal failure or dermatitis herpetiformis, and patients before or after radioactive iodine treatment must not use this medicine.
  • Before using this medicine, seriously ill patients (such as patients with extensive burns), those who have had thyroid disease, and pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not use it as an ophthalmic preparation or take it orally.
  • Be careful not to let it get into the eyes, and if it does, rinse immediately with clean water.
  • Do not mix it with other preparations.
  • Wash and disinfect the affected area thoroughly.
  • When it is used on severe wounds, use distilled water for injection or sterile purified water as the diluent, not tap water or purified water.
  • Since soaps weaken the disinfecting action of this medicine, wash them off thoroughly before use.

Possible side effects

  • If difficulty breathing, flushing, hives, or iododerma rarely occurs, if pain, itching, an irritated feeling, rash, redness, or dermatitis sometimes occurs, or if a burning sensation, skin ulcer, contact dermatitis, or skin discoloration rarely occurs, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not use this medicine together with hydrogen peroxide.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when using it together with lithium preparations, chlorhexidine, sulfadiazine and silver compounds, alkalis, preparations containing mercury, or enzyme-based wound healing preparations.

Oral medicine (MFDS 200511037)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 200511037. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used as a smoking cessation aid for the relief of nicotine withdrawal symptoms in nicotine dependence.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used as a smoking cessation aid for the relief of nicotine withdrawal symptoms in nicotine dependence.

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 200511037. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults and elderly people (the aged), when they feel an urge to smoke, place 1 tablet of this medicine in the mouth and take it by sucking it slowly without chewing or swallowing it. At first, take 1 tablet of this medicine every 1 to 2 hours. Usually 8 to 12 tablets a day are taken, and do not exceed a maximum of 25 tablets a day. Take this medicine in the following order. Place 1 tablet of this medicine in the mouth and suck it until a strong taste is felt. Then place it between the gum and the cheek, and when the taste fades, repeat in the same way, sucking until it dissolves completely. The treatment period is at least 3 months; from 3 months onward the dose should be reduced in stages, and treatment should be stopped when the dose of this medicine has been reduced to 1 to 2 tablets a day. In general, nicotine replacement products such as this medicine are not recommended for use for more than 6 months.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with unstable angina or worsening angina, patients who have had a myocardial infarction within the last 3 months, patients in the late acute infarction period, patients with clinically relevant cardiac arrhythmias including severe cardiac arrhythmias, patients with severe cardiovascular disease such as systemic hypertension or peripheral vascular disease, patients with acute stroke or recent cerebrovascular disease, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, children and adolescents under 18 years of age, and non-smokers and occasional smokers must not use this medicine.
  • Before using this medicine, patients with cardiovascular disease such as active esophagitis, oral (inside the mouth) and pharyngeal inflammation, gastritis, peptic ulcer, occlusive (closed and blocked) arterial disease, stable angina, heart failure, decompensated heart failure, myocardial infarction, cardiac arrhythmia, vasospasm, uncontrolled high blood pressure, or arterial bypass grafting or angioplasty, elderly people, patients with renal or hepatic failure, patients with diabetes, hyperthyroidism, or pheochromocytoma, and people receiving anticonvulsant treatment or with a history of epilepsy should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If insomnia, dizziness, headache, tremor, nausea, vomiting, indigestion, upper abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal distension, hiccups, gastritis, dry mouth, stomatitis, esophagitis, oral discomfort, difficulty swallowing, belching, excessive salivation, pharyngitis, cough, sore throat, difficulty breathing, palpitations, atrial arrhythmia, tachycardia (rapid pulse), hypersensitivity, angioneurotic edema, urticaria, ulcerative stomatitis, anaphylaxis, asthenia, fatigue, malaise, or influenza-like illness occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.Occasionally, mild throat irritation, increased salivation, hiccups, indigestion, or heartburn may occur at the beginning of treatment.

Interactions

  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you use it together with paracetamol, caffeine, imipramine, oxazepam, pentazocine, propranolol, theophylline, warfarin, estrogen, lignocaine, phenacetin, insulin, adrenergic antagonists (prazosin, labetalol, etc.), flecainide, adrenergic agonists (isoprenaline, phenylephrine), propoxyphene, furosemide diuretics, H2 antagonists, beta blockers, theophylline, tacrine, clozapine, or ropinirole.

Oral medicine (MFDS 202400752)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202400752. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used for fever and pain due to colds, headache, neuralgia, muscle pain, menstrual pain, and pain from sprains. This medicine is used for toothache, joint pain, and rheumatic pain.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for fever and pain due to colds, headache, neuralgia, muscle pain, menstrual pain, and pain from s

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202400752. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Children aged 12 years and under take the following recommended 1-time dose every 4 to 6 hours as needed. For the recommended 1-time dose by age group, refer to the approved labeling. Take the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible period, and do not take it more than 5 times a day (75 mg/kg). If the body weight is known, it is more appropriate to take a dose based on body weight (10 to 15 mg/kg).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported, and if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily amount of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products that contain acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe renal disorder or severe cardiac dysfunction, and patients in whom non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs induce asthma attacks, that is, patients with aspirin asthma or those who have experienced it, must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, those who have experienced hypersensitivity or peptic ulcer, patients with liver or renal disorder or those who have experienced it, patients with blood abnormalities or those who have experienced them, patients with a tendency to bleed, patients with cardiac dysfunction, patients with bronchial asthma, the elderly, children under 2 years of age, and pregnant or breastfeeding women should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Without the instruction of a doctor or pharmacist, do not take it for pain for more than 10 days in adults or more than 5 days in children.
  • Do not take it for fever for more than 3 days.
  • If pain or fever persists or worsens, or if new symptoms appear, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Children and the elderly should take the minimum necessary dose and watch for adverse reactions.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms such as difficulty breathing, reddening of the whole body, swelling of the blood vessels, or urticaria, or asthma attacks, thrombocytopenia, granulocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, methemoglobinemia, reduced platelet function such as prolonged bleeding time, cyanosis, hypersensitivity symptoms such as facial swelling, sweating, or low blood pressure, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation, rash, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), elevated AST, elevated ALT, or fixed drug eruption occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • People taking barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol must not take this medicine.
  • Do not take it together with other anti-inflammatory analgesics.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients taking warfarin long term and patients taking lithium or thiazide diuretics should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Category

How it works

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, co

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201903798. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults aged 15 years and older take 2 capsules per dose, 3 times a day 30 minutes after meals.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.

  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine and those who have experienced it, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, and infants under 3 months of age should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, people who are physically weak, people with an allergic constitution, people who have experienced allergies to medicines (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), patients with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.), difficulty urinating, high fever, gastrointestinal problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain, ulcers or bleeding problems, smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, or emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough that lasts 1 week or more or recurs, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash, or persistent headache, and children under 2 years of age should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration exactly.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so be careful when driving or operating machinery.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after 5 to 6 doses, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • If rash, redness, itching, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, swelling, difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling, and chest tightness immediately after taking it, together with pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash, redness, and burn-like blisters appearing on the skin all over the body, in the mouth, or on the mucous membranes of the eyes), acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, asthma, hepatic dysfunction (general listlessness, jaundice), or interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, breathlessness, difficulty breathing, and fever) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussive expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness remedies, allergy remedies).
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking it together with diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.

At a glance

Category

How it works

This drug is used for reducing fever when fever occurs due to acute upper respiratory tract infection.

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 200608160. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Children aged 6 months and older take 0.4 to 0.6 mL/kg (5 to 7 mg/kg) per dose as needed at intervals of 4 to 6 hours, not exceeding a maximum of 4 doses a day (28 mg/kg). If the body weight is known, it is more appropriate to take the dose based on body weight, so refer to the approved product information for the recommended doses by age group.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.
  • Taking this medicine may cause serious and potentially fatal gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, peptic ulcer, severe blood disorders, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, severe heart failure, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma or a history of it, patients with or a history of asthma, urticaria, or allergy caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients being treated for pain before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, and pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and nursing mothers must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, those with a history of peptic ulcer, patients with or a history of blood disorders, patients with a bleeding tendency, patients with or a history of liver disorder or kidney disorder, patients with heart failure, high blood pressure, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people and children, patients with stomach cancer, and people taking low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If any of the following occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rarely shock (chills, difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, etc.), aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stool, gastritis, pancreatitis; occasionally loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort; very rarely dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, constipation, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome) or Lyell's syndrome (toxic epidermal necrolysis); drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency, jaundice, elevated GOT, GPT and AL-P, induction of asthma attacks, urticaria, eczema, purpura; occasionally rash, itching, visual disturbances such as misty vision and dimmed vision, hearing loss, tinnitus, taste disturbance, aseptic meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness), autoimmune diseases (SLE, MCTD); rarely drop in blood pressure, rise in blood pressure, palpitations; rarely acute renal failure (oliguria, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, decreased urine volume, generalized edema, shortness of breath, listlessness), heart failure, Conn's syndrome of unknown frequency, occasionally periorbital edema, and very rarely malaise, fever, or nosebleed.

Interactions

  • Do not use together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you use it together with glucocorticoids, alcohol, digoxin, phenytoin, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, sulfonylureas, diuretics, antihypertensives, ACE inhibitors, furosemide, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, or coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin).

Apply 0.25 to 0.66 g of the cream (23 to 62 mg as lidocaine) 5 to 15 minutes before sexual intercourse. The amount and the application time differ from person to person, so use the lowest effective amount and do not use more than 2 g (184 mg as lidocaine) within 24 hours.

  • It is preferable not to apply it to the same area repeatedly.

Possible side effects

  • If a rash or irritation appears in the user or in the partner, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

How to take it

Adults and elderly people (the aged), when they feel an urge to smoke, place 1 tablet of this medicine in the mouth and take it by sucking it slowly without chewing or swallowing it. At first, take 1 tablet of this medicine every 1 to 2 hours. Usually 8 to 12 tablets a day are taken, and do not exceed a maximum of 25 tablets a day. Take this medicine in the following order. Place 1 tablet of this medicine in the mouth and suck it until a strong taste is felt. Then place it between the gum and the cheek, and when the taste fades, repeat in the same way, sucking until it dissolves completely. The treatment period is at least 3 months; from 3 months onward the dose should be reduced in stages, and treatment should be stopped when the dose of this medicine has been reduced to 1 to 2 tablets a day. In general, nicotine replacement products such as this medicine are not recommended for use for more than 6 months.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with unstable angina or worsening angina, patients who have had a myocardial infarction within the last 3 months, patients in the late acute infarction period, patients with clinically relevant cardiac arrhythmias including severe cardiac arrhythmias, patients with severe cardiovascular disease such as systemic hypertension or peripheral vascular disease, patients with acute stroke or recent cerebrovascular disease, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, children and adolescents under 18 years of age, and non-smokers and occasional smokers must not use this medicine.

  • While using this medicine, do not take (use) suppositories, ointments or creams containing dl-methylephedrine hydrochloride, scopolia extract or glycyrrhizic acid, or antihypertensive medicines or antidepressants.

Category

How it works

This medicine is used for chronic constipation, constipation in infants, young children, and children, and constipation

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201802080. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For chronic constipation, adults take 15 to 30 mL a day before breakfast for the first 2 to 3 days, and thereafter continue with 10 to 15 mL a day. In severe cases up to 45 mL may be taken. Children (7 to 14 years) take 15 mL a day for the first 2 to 3 days and thereafter continue with 10 mL a day. Young children (1 to 6 years) take 5 to 10 mL a day, and infants (under 12 months) take 5 mL a day.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease), gastrointestinal obstruction, abdominal pain of unknown cause, a low-galactose diet (galactosemia), or gastrointestinal perforation or a risk of it, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, infants, young children and children, the elderly, and patients with diabetes, fructose intolerance, fluid and electrolyte imbalance, acute gastritis or chronic constipation should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If loose stools or diarrhea occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Belching, cramping abdominal discomfort, and occasionally borborygmi, abdominal bloating, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea, and vomiting may occur.

Interactions

  • Patients who take α-glucosidase inhibitors such as acarbose, broad-spectrum antibiotics, diuretics, corticosteroids, amphotericin B, cardiac glycosides, or antacids should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 200713754. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

Apply an appropriate amount to the affected area (diseased site) several times a day.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be used by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by patients with thyroid dysfunction (especially nodular goiter, endemic goiter, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, etc.), renal failure, dermatitis herpetiformis, by patients before or after radioactive iodine treatment, or by newborns and infants under 6 months of age.

  • Do not mix it with other preparations for use.

This medicine is used for the relief of pain from headache, toothache, pain after tooth extraction, sore throat, earache, joint pain, neuralgia, back pain, muscle pain, stiff shoulders, bruise pain, fracture pain, sprain pain, menstrual pain (period pain), and pain from injury, and for the reduction of fever when there are chills and fever.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for the relief of pain from headache, toothache, pain after tooth extraction, sore throat, earache

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202401380. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over take 1 packet at a time, those aged 11 years and over but under 15 years take 2/3 of a packet at a time, those aged 7 years and over but under 11 years take 1/2 of a packet at a time, those aged 3 years and over but under 7 years take 1/3 of a packet at a time, and those aged 2 years and over but under 3 years take 1/4 of a packet at a time, 3 times a day, avoiding an empty stomach. Leave an interval of at least 4 hours between doses.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported, and if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily amount of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products that contain acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or those who have experienced it, those who have experienced asthma when taking this medicine or its components or other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, infants under 3 months of age, and children under 2 years of age must not take this medicine.Before taking this medicine, children under 2 years of age in cases where it is strictly necessary, infants infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza and children under 15 years of age, those with an allergic constitution, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant, breastfeeding women, those who have experienced allergic symptoms caused by medicines such as fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, or itching, elderly people, and physically weak people or people with a high fever should consult a doctor or pharmacist.Before taking this medicine, people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, or high blood pressure, and people with persistent or recurring gastrointestinal problems such as heartburn, gastric discomfort, or stomach pain or with ulcer or bleeding problems should consult a doctor or pharmacist.If symptoms do not improve after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.Children should take it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.Do not take it continuously over a long period.Strictly observe the specified dosage and administration.

Possible side effects

  • If shock (anaphylaxis), which rarely may appear immediately after taking the medicine with urticaria, swelling, and chest tightness along with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing, or mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), asthma, or liver function disorders such as general fatigue and jaundice occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • While taking this medicine, do not take other antipyretic analgesics, cold remedies, or sedatives.Before taking this medicine, people receiving antidiabetic medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, etc. should consult a doctor or pharmacist.Patients receiving barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol should consult a doctor or pharmacist.Do not drink alcohol while taking it.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for constipation.

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202300044. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults and children aged 8 years and over take 20 to 40 mL (1 to 2 sachets) a day, based on a package unit of 1 sachet (20 mL). Depending on the symptoms, children in particular may take 20 mL (1 sachet) every two days. Dissolve 20 mL (1 sachet) of this medicine in water to make 50 mL and take it. It is recommended to take it in the morning. Children from 6 months to 7 years of age, based on a package unit of 1 sachet (8 mL), take 8 mL (1 sachet) a day at 6 months to 1 year of age, 8 to 16 mL (1 to 2 sachets) a day at 1 to 4 years of age, and 16 to 32 mL (2 to 4 sachets) a day at 4 to 7 years of age. When 1 sachet (8 mL) a day is taken, take it in the morning, and when more than 1 sachet (8 mL) a day is taken, divide it between morning and evening. Dissolve 8 mL (1 sachet) of this medicine in water to make 50 mL and take it.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by patients with inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, etc.) or toxic megacolon, by patients with intestinal perforation or at risk of intestinal perforation, by patients who have or are suspected of having intestinal obstruction, by patients with intestinal stricture, or by patients with abdominal pain of unknown cause.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the user is a pregnant woman or a woman who may be pregnant or a breast-feeding woman, has acute constipation that is not caused by a change in lifestyle habits or acute constipation accompanied by pain, fever or abdominal distension, has irritable bowel syndrome, or has a hypersensitivity reaction to macrogol (polyethylene glycol).
  • In children, do not give this medicine for 3 months or more, and do not give this medicine for a long period without the judgment of a doctor.

Possible side effects

  • In adults, if abdominal pain and abdominal distension, diarrhea or nausea appears, if vomiting, urgent defecation or fecal incontinence uncommonly appears, if electrolyte disturbance (hyponatremia, hypokalemia, etc.), dehydration or erythema appears at an unknown frequency, or if a hypersensitivity reaction (itching, rash, facial edema, angioedema, urticaria, anaphylactic shock, etc.) very rarely appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • In children, if abdominal pain, diarrhea or perianal pain caused by diarrhea appears, if vomiting, abdominal distension or nausea uncommonly appears, or if a hypersensitivity reaction (hypersensitivity, angioedema, urticaria, rash, itching, etc.) appears at an unknown frequency, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (occurring at a young age), osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), fever and pain due to colds, low back pain, dysmenorrhea, postoperative pain, ankylosing spondylitis, headache, toothache, muscle pain, neuralgia, acute gout, psoriatic arthritis, soft tissue injuries (sprains, contusions (bruises)), and non-articular rheumatic diseases (tendinitis, tenosynovitis, bursitis).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (occurring at a young age), osteoarthritis

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202402790. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200 to 600 mg orally as 1 dose, 3 to 4 times a day. Up to a maximum of 4200 mg may be given in 1 day. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, 30 to 40 mg per kg of body weight is given orally in 1 day, divided into 3 to 4 doses. For mild to moderate pain and colds, 200 to 400 mg is taken orally as 1 dose, 3 to 4 times a day. Increase or decrease the amount appropriately according to age and symptoms. For the single dose and the maximum daily dose for children, refer to the approved product information.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, patients with gastrointestinal ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding or those who have experienced it, patients with severe blood abnormalities, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, or high blood pressure, patients with bronchial asthma or those who have experienced it, patients with asthma, rhinitis, nasal polyps, urticaria, or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors) or those who have experienced them, patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, and patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with blood abnormalities or those who have experienced them, patients with a bleeding tendency, patients with liver cirrhosis, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, or heart disease or those who have experienced them, patients with high blood pressure, patients with hypersensitivity, patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease, patients with ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, elderly people and children, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, and people who take low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not take more than the recommended dose.

Possible side effects

  • If any of the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: shock, anaphylactoid reactions, heartburn, chills, difficulty breathing, a drop in blood pressure, decreased hematocrit and hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, decreased granulocytes, white blood cells and platelets, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, vomiting of blood, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, thirst, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, mouth ulcers, constipation, black stools, skin-mucosa-eye syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), photosensitivity reactions, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, exfoliative dermatitis, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, hepatitis, jaundice, elevated GOT, GPT and alkaline phosphatase (ALP), asthma attacks, hives, eczema, purple spots, rash, itching, asthma, bronchoconstriction, difficulty breathing or wheezing, scotoma, deafness, ringing in the ears, taste disturbance, vertigo, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness, aseptic meningitis or meningitis (symptoms such as severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever, or disturbance of consciousness), a drop in blood pressure, a rise in blood pressure, palpitations, heart failure, myocardial infarction or angina, acute renal failure, decreased urination, blood in the urine, protein in the urine, elevated BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath, lethargy, Kounis syndrome of unknown frequency, swelling around the eyes, facial edema, malaise, fever, nosebleed, swelling, and peripheral edema.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, naproxen derivatives, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking it together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (NSAIDs), ACE inhibitors, lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin, etc.), or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

  • If eye irritation rarely appears, stop using this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200-600 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. Up to a maximum of 3,200 mg a day may be taken. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30 to 40 mg per kg of body weight per dose, in 3 to 4 divided doses a day. For mild to moderate pain and for colds, adults take 200 to 400 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. The dose may be increased or decreased as appropriate according to age and symptoms. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years take 200 to 250 mg (10 to 12.5 mL) per dose, those aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg (7.5 to 10 mL) per dose, those aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg (5 to 7.5 mL) per dose, and those aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg (2.5 to 5 mL) per dose, 3 to 4 times a day, and it is advisable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years may take up to 1,000 mg (50 mL) a day, those aged 7 to 10 years up to 800 mg (40 mL), those aged 3 to 6 years up to 600 mg (30 mL), and those aged 1 to 2 years up to 400 mg (20 mL).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, severe blood abnormalities, severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma, patients who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, breastfeeding women, patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Do not take more than the recommended dose.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with blood abnormalities or a bleeding tendency, patients with liver cirrhosis, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, heart disease, high blood pressure, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people, children under 2 years of age, pregnant women, and patients with chickenpox should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • When taking it for a cold, take it for no more than 5 days as a rule, and without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist do not take it for pain for 10 days or more (adults) or 5 days or more (children), and do not take it for fever for 3 days or more.

  • If shock (difficulty breathing, fall in blood pressure, etc.), blood disorders such as decreased hematocrit, decreased hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function or eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, vomiting of blood, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal distension, oral ulcers, constipation, black stools, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, exfoliative dermatitis, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, hepatitis, jaundice, abnormal liver function, liver disorder, hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reaction, asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purple spots, visual disturbance, deafness, ringing in the ears, taste abnormality, vertigo, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness, aseptic meningitis or meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever or impaired consciousness), acute renal failure, decreased urination, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN or blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath or listlessness, Kounis syndrome of unknown frequency, swelling around the eyes, facial swelling, malaise, fever, nosebleed, swelling or peripheral edema appear, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202501643. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over and adults take 1 bottle at a time, three times a day, 30 minutes after meals. If necessary it may be taken at bedtime, and as a rule the interval between doses should be at least 4 hours.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.
  • If severe skin adverse reactions such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis occur, stop taking it and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or a history of it, people who have had asthma when taking this medicine or its ingredients, other antipyretic analgesics, or cold remedies, infants under 3 months of age, breastfeeding women, and patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure or severe acute or chronic kidney disease and renal failure must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist in the following cases: patients with hypersensitivity to caramel or people who have experienced allergic reactions to it; infants and children under 15 years of age who have had or are suspected of having chickenpox or influenza; symptoms of ischemic colitis (sudden abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, etc.); people with an allergic constitution; people who have had allergic reactions (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.); people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.), or difficulty urinating; elderly people; people who are physically weak or have a high fever; people with stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems; women who are pregnant or may be pregnant; breastfeeding women; patients with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough with excessive phlegm, a cough lasting 1 week or longer or recurring, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever and rash or a persistent headache; and children under 2 years of age.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the specified dosage and administration carefully.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.

Possible side effects

  • If rash, redness, itching, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, high anion gap metabolic acidosis, rarely shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling, or chest tightness immediately after taking it, together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (accompanied by high fever, with severe symptoms such as rash and redness and burn-like blistering appearing on the skin over the whole body, the mouth, or the mucous membranes of the eyes), asthma, generalized lassitude, jaundice, interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, and fever), or symptoms of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (sudden severe headache, thunderclap headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinson drugs, etc.), antitussive-expectorants, other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines), or preparations containing diphenhydramine.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.
  • If taken together with diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol or flucloxacillin, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Who should ask first

How to take it

Adults and children aged 12 years and older take 10 mg a day; children aged 2 to under 12 years take 10 mg a day if they weigh 30 kg or more and 5 mg a day if they weigh less than 30 kg, taken 1 time a day. Patients who are sensitive to adverse reactions take it in divided doses in the morning and evening. The dose may be increased or decreased appropriately according to age and symptoms. Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or to hydroxyzine or piperazine derivatives or those who have experienced it, patients with renal failure, pregnant women and women who may be pregnant, breastfeeding women, infants under 2 years of age, and patients with fructose intolerance should not take this medicine.

  • Do not take more than the specified dose when driving or operating machinery.
  • It is advisable not to take this medicine for 3 to 5 days before an allergen intradermal skin test.

Possible side effects

  • If drowsiness, headache, vasculitis, photosensitivity, dizziness, joint pain, pharyngitis, cough, nosebleed, bronchospasm, hearing abnormalities, visual abnormalities, occasionally elevated BUN, glycosuria, or blood in the urine, or rarely difficulty urinating, bedwetting, or urinary retention occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take this medicine together with theophylline or ritonavir.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to use the eye drops

As needed, instill 1 drop into each eye at a time, several times a day. Gently pull the lower eyelid down and, while looking up, instill one drop into the lower conjunctival sac.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine must not use this medicine.
  • Before using this medicine, patients with severe eye pain, patients who have experienced allergic reactions to eye drops (redness of the eye, itching, swelling, rash, congestion and reddening, etc.), and patients with glaucoma should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If the symptoms become worse or last for 3 days or more, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • Use this medicine for instillation into the eye only.
  • Wash your hands thoroughly before use.
  • In the case of single-use products, discard the first 1 to 2 drops without instilling them when first using it.
  • This is to remove any container fragments produced when opening it.
  • Since it is a single-use preparation, use it only 1 time after opening, and discard the remaining solution and the container after instillation.
  • If the tip of the container touches the eyelid or eyelashes, the solution may become contaminated or cloudy from eye mucus or mold, so be careful, and do not use it if it has become cloudy.
  • To prevent contamination, avoid sharing it with others as far as possible.
  • This medicine can be used even while wearing contact lenses.

Possible side effects

  • If eye irritation rarely appears, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • When using this medicine at the same time as other eye drops, instill this medicine about 10 minutes after using the other eye drops.

Apply to the affected area (diseased site) 1 to 2 times a day. Category

How it works

This medicine is used to relieve all the symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, cough,

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201907024. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over and adults take 2 capsules at a time 3 times a day, and those aged 8 years to under 15 years take 1 capsule at a time 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.
  • If severe skin adverse reactions such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis occur, stop taking it and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine or those who have experienced it, those who have experienced asthma when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants under 3 months of age, and patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, the following should consult a doctor or pharmacist: infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza; those in whom symptoms of ischemic colitis (sudden abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, etc.) appear in relation to the pseudoephedrine component; people with an allergic constitution or who have experienced an allergic reaction to a medicine (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.); people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.) or difficulty urinating; the elderly; people with a weak body or a high fever; people with persistent or recurrent stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems; pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women; and children under 2 years of age.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with a cough (smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough with excessive phlegm, a cough lasting or recurring for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, a cough accompanied by fever, rash or persistent headache) should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If the symptoms do not improve after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • When used for a child, use it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, rarely shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling, and chest tightness immediately after taking the medicine, along with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome) (accompanied by high fever, with severe symptoms such as rash and redness and blistering like burns that may appear on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes), asthma, liver function disorder (general fatigue and jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes take on a yellow color) may appear), interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, and fever), or posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (sudden severe headache, thunderclap headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance, etc. may appear) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussives and expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).People who stopped taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) within the past 2 weeks must not take this medicine.Before taking this medicine, people receiving antidiabetic medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, etc. should consult a doctor or pharmacist.Patients who have been given barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol should consult a doctor or pharmacist.Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.

payloads.summary: This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendini
payloads.content:

Oral medicine (MFDS 199902599)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199902599. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendinitis, acute gout, dysmenorrhea and bursitis, skeletal muscle disorders (sprain, contusion (bruise), trauma (wound), lumbosacral pain (low back pain)), postoperative pain (aches), migraine, and pain after tooth extraction (pulling out a tooth).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendini

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199902599. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, adults take 1 to 2 tablets (275 to 550 mg) at a time, twice a day (every 12 hours). For acute gout, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 8 hours until the attack subsides. For skeletal muscle disorders, pain after surgery, pain after tooth extraction (having a tooth pulled), dysmenorrhea, tendinitis (inflammation of a tendon), and bursitis (inflammation of the lubricating sac), take 2 tablets (550 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 6 to 8 hours, and do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg). For migraine, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose); if necessary, 1 to 2 more tablets (275 to 550 mg) may be taken a day, and these are taken 30 minutes after the initial dose (the first dose). Do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe renal disorder or severe high blood pressure, patients hypersensitive to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as aspirin, patients who have had asthma, rhinitis (nasal inflammation), nasal polyps, urticaria or an allergic reaction caused by aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors) or those who have experienced them, patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, and children aged 2 years or under must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women and women who may be pregnant, children, the elderly, those who have experienced peptic ulcer, those who have experienced blood abnormalities, patients with a tendency to bleed, patients with liver disorder or those who have experienced it, patients with renal disorder or those who have experienced it, and patients with cardiac dysfunction, high blood pressure, bronchial asthma, systemic lupus erythematosus or mixed connective tissue disease should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If an increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke, serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions that may be fatal such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcers, and perforation, rarely shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, a fall in blood pressure, bradycardia (a slow pulse), cold sweat, swelling), PIE syndrome (pulmonary infiltration with eosinophilia: accompanied by fever, wheezing, coughing, and phlegm), urticaria, occasionally hypersensitivity symptoms such as rash or itching, hematemesis (vomiting of blood), gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation, aseptic meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness), eczema, sweating, purpura (purple spots), photosensitivity, hair loss, redness (turning red from congestion), necrolysis, erythema multiforme (red spots of various shapes), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), urticaria, epidermolysis bullosa, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, fixed drug eruption, exfoliative dermatitis, or rarely blood disorders such as agranulocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic (red-blood-cell-destroying) anemia, or reduced platelet function (prolongation of bleeding time) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Occasionally stomach discomfort, stomach pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, indigestion, heartburn, diarrhea, constipation, or stomatitis (inflammation inside the mouth), and rarely abdominal bloating, black stools, dry mouth, elevated GOT and GPT values, jaundice, hepatitis, kidney disorder, nephritis, hematuria, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, proteinuria (urine containing protein), renal failure, ringing in the ears, hearing impairment, visual impairment, swelling, difficulty breathing, palpitations (a pounding heart), myasthenia (muscle weakness), congestive heart failure, eosinophilic pneumonia, anaphylactoid reactions, menstrual disorders, chills (feeling cold and shivering) and fever, vasculitis, high blood sugar, or low blood sugar may occur.

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, co

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202008429. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over take 1 sachet (20 mL), those aged 11 years and over but under 15 years take 2/3 of a sachet, those aged 7 years and over but under 11 years take 1/2 of a sachet, those aged 3 years and over but under 7 years take 1/3 of a sachet, and those aged 2 years and over but under 3 years take 1/4 of a sachet, three times a day, 30 minutes after meals.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when they take this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.
  • If severe skin adverse reactions such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis occur, stop taking it and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • This medicine contains aspartame, which is metabolized to phenylalanine in the body, so patients with phenylketonuria who need to restrict their phenylalanine intake must not take it.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine or with such a history, people who have had asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, infants (newborns) under 3 months of age, and patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if you are a child aged 3 months and over but under 2 years, an infant or a child under 15 years of age who is infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, a person with an allergic constitution or a history of allergy to medicines, a person with liver, kidney, heart, or thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.), or difficulty urinating (passing urine), an elderly person, a person who is physically weak or who has a high fever, a person with persistent or recurring gastrointestinal problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain or with ulcers or bleeding problems, a pregnant woman or a woman who may be pregnant, a breastfeeding woman, or a person with symptoms such as smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough that persists or recurs for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash, or a persistent headache.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • When administering it to children, do so under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • If symptoms do not improve after 5 to 6 doses, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness (turning red from congestion), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema (swelling), difficulty urinating (passing urine), persistent or severe thirst, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling, and chest tightness immediately after taking the medicine, along with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome: accompanied by high fever, with severe symptoms such as rash and redness and blistering like burns), asthma, general fatigue, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes take on a yellow color), interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, and fever), symptoms of ischemic colitis associated with the pseudoephedrine component (sudden abdominal pain, rectal bleeding), or posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (sudden severe headache, thunderclap headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance, etc.) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussives and expectorants (cough and phlegm medicines), other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis [nasal inflammation], motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • People who are within 2 weeks of stopping MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) must not take this medicine.
  • People who are being given other medicines such as barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants and alcohol, diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, or steroids should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Adults use an appropriate amount, enough to cover the affected area fully to its edge, 5 times a day for 5 days. Limit the treatment period with this medicine to 5 days or less. Start the treatment as soon as possible, right when the first symptoms and signs appear.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with skin infections (tuberculosis, syphilis, candidiasis, ringworm, shingles, chickenpox, vaccinia, scabies, pubic lice), patients with a damaged immune system (bone marrow transplantation or AIDS), patients with eczematous otitis externa with a perforated eardrum, ulcers (excluding Behcet's disease), burns and frostbite of deep second degree or worse, perioral dermatitis, acne vulgaris, or rosacea, breastfeeding women, children under 18 years of age, and patients who have or have had a myocardial infarction must not use this medicine.

  • Use it only on cold sores on the lips or around the mouth, and do not use it in the eyes, nose, mouth, or on the genitals.
  • Do not use it on people who have no signs or symptoms.
  • Do not use it for the purpose of preventing transmission to others or preventing recurrent herpes simplex infection.
  • Do not use this medicine as a base for diluting it or mixing it with other medicines.

  • If dryness or peeling of the skin commonly occurs, a temporary burning sensation or numbness sometimes occurs, or rarely erythema, pigmentation, application-site reactions including the signs and symptoms of inflammation, contact dermatitis, or impetigo contagiosa, folliculitis, candidiasis, ringworm, folliculitis, boils, skin irritation, stinging pain, fever, a burning sensation, rash, redness, flushing, itching, dry skin, pustular dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, prickly heat, sudamina, worsening of wounds, pressure sores, pustulosis, or, when used on the skin of the eyelids, a rise in intraocular pressure or glaucoma (blurred vision, impaired eyesight) occurs, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Systemic absorption may cause reversible Cushing's syndrome, high blood sugar, glucose in the urine, and visual impairment.

Who should ask first

How to apply it

For sterilizing and disinfecting the hands and arms of the surgeon, put 5 mL of this medicine on the hands and arms, rub it in well for about 5 minutes to produce plenty of lather, and then rinse it off thoroughly with running water. For sterilizing and disinfecting the surgical site, apply this medicine directly or use an appropriate amount, rub it in well to produce plenty of lather, and then wipe it off with sterile gauze.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be used by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by patients with thyroid dysfunction (especially nodular goiter, endemic goiter, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, etc.), renal failure, dermatitis herpetiformis, by patients before or after radioactive iodine treatment, or by newborns and infants under 6 months of age.

  • Do not use it for the eyes or internally.
  • Be careful to keep it out of the eyes, and if it does get into the eyes, rinse them immediately with clean water.
  • Do not mix it with other preparations for use.
  • Because soaps weaken the germicidal action of this medicine, wash them off thoroughly before use.
  • Wash and disinfect the affected area thoroughly.
  • When it is used on a severe wound, use distilled water for injection or sterile purified water as the diluent, and do not use tap water or purified water.

  • If symptoms of shock (difficulty breathing, flushing, urticaria, itching, swelling, heartburn and at the same time pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, shortness of breath, etc.) or iododerma rarely appear, if pain, a feeling of irritation, rash, redness or dermatitis occasionally appears, or if a burning sensation, skin ulcer, contact dermatitis or skin discoloration rarely appears, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not use this medicine together with hydrogen peroxide.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when using it together with lithium preparations, chlorhexidine, sulfadiazine and silver compounds, alkalis, preparations containing mercury, or enzyme-based wound healing preparations.

Category

How it works

This medicine is used for the relief of the various symptoms of the common cold (sore throat (pain in the throat), chill

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201900992. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over and adults take 1 packet (a single dose) at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. The interval between doses should be 4 hours.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants (babies) under 3 months of age, and people who are taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) or are within 2 weeks of having stopped them must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants and children under 15 years of age who have or are suspected of having a chickenpox or influenza infection, people with an allergic constitution, people who have experienced allergic symptoms (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, edema (swelling), gastroduodenal ulcer and the like, the elderly, people with a weak body or a high fever, people with persistent or recurring stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach (upper abdominal) discomfort or stomach pain, or with ulcer or bleeding problems, women who are pregnant or may be pregnant, breastfeeding women, and children under 2 years of age should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, swelling (puffiness), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia; rarely shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling (puffiness), and chest tightness right after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing); Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome); toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome) (severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash and redness (reddening of the skin) and blistering like burns appearing on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes); asthma; liver function disorder (general lethargy, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes turn yellow)); interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever); pseudoaldosteronism; or myopathy (muscle disease).

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with antitussives (which stop coughing) and expectorants (phlegm medicines), other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis (nasal inflammation), motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • If it is taken together with diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol, potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, etacrynic acid), or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide), consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.
