Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over take 1 packet (75 mL) at a time, those aged 11 years and over but under 15 years take 2/3 of a packet (50 mL) at a time, those aged 7 years and over but under 11 years take 1/2 of a packet (37.5 mL) at a time, those aged 3 years and over but under 7 years take 1/3 of a packet (25 mL) at a time, and those aged 2 years and over but under 3 years take 1/4 of a packet (18.7 mL) at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine or with such a history, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, infants under 3 months of age, and people who are taking an MAO inhibitor (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) or are within 2 weeks of stopping one must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants under 2 years of age, infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, elderly people, people who are physically weak, people with an allergic constitution, people with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, edema, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.), difficulty urinating, or high fever, people with persistent or recurring gastrointestinal problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain or with ulcers or bleeding problems, and patients with smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough that persists or recurs for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash, or a persistent headache should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • When administering it to children, do so under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, shock symptoms (urticaria, edema and chest tightness immediately after taking the medicine, together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat and difficulty breathing), Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis (severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash and redness and blistering like a burn), asthma, generalized listlessness, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes turning yellow), interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, breathlessness, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.), or a decrease in urine volume, swelling of the face, hands and feet, heaviness of the eyelids, stiffening of the hands, a rise in blood pressure or headache, or myopathy (weakness, cramps in the limbs, paralysis, etc.) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other products containing acetaminophen, MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussives (which stop coughing) and expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis (nasal inflammation), motion sickness remedies, anti-allergy remedies).
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants or alcohol, potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, etacrynic acid), or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide).
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.

Oral medicine (MFDS 199804309)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199804309. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), fever and pain due to a cold, low back pain, dysmenorrhea, post-operative pain and ankylosing spondylitis, headache, toothache, muscle pain, neuralgia, acute gout, psoriatic arthritis, soft tissue injury (sprain, contusion), and non-articular rheumatic diseases (tendinitis, tenosynovitis, bursitis).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint diseas

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199804309. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 1/2 tablet to 1.5 tablets (200 to 600 mg) per dose 3 to 4 times a day, up to a maximum of 3200 mg a day. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30 to 40 mg per kg of body weight a day, divided into 3 to 4 doses; for mild to moderate pain or a cold, adults take 1/2 tablet to 1 tablet (200 to 400 mg) per dose 3 to 4 times a day. Children aged 11 to 14 years take 200 to 250 mg per dose, children aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg per dose, children aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg per dose, and children aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg per dose, orally 3 to 4 times a day. For children weighing less than 30 kg the daily amount must not exceed 500 mg, and it is preferable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. Do not take more than the recommended amount.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by patients who have or have had gastrointestinal ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding, by patients with severe blood abnormality, severe liver impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency or severe high blood pressure, by patients who have or have had bronchial asthma, by patients who have or have had hypersensitivity such as asthma, urticaria or an allergic reaction to aspirin or another non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesic (including COX-2 inhibitors), by patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, by pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, by patients taking high-dose methotrexate as anticancer therapy, or by patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the user has or has had blood abnormality, has a bleeding tendency, has or has had cirrhosis or liver impairment, has or has had renal impairment, has cardiac insufficiency or heart disease, high blood pressure, a history of hypersensitivity, systemic lupus erythematosus or mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, is elderly or a child, is a pregnant woman or a breast-feeding woman, or is taking low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke.
  • Without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist, do not take it for pain for 10 days or more (adults) or 5 days or more (children), and do not take it for fever for 3 days or more.

Possible side effects

  • If any of the following appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: symptoms of shock (heartburn, chills, difficulty breathing, fall in blood pressure); blood disorders such as decreased hematocrit, decreased hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time) and eosinophilia; peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, hematemesis, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, thirst, stomatitis, abdominal distension, oral ulcer, constipation and black stools; mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), photosensitivity reaction, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, exfoliative dermatitis and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis; hepatitis, jaundice, hepatic dysfunction such as increases in GOT, GPT and ALP, and liver impairment; hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reaction, asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purpura, rash, itching, asthma, bronchoconstriction, difficulty breathing or wheezing; visual disturbance such as a blind area of the visual field, hearing loss, tinnitus and abnormal taste; vertigo, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness; aseptic meningitis or meningitis (symptoms such as severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever or disturbance of consciousness); rise in blood pressure, palpitations, heart failure, myocardial infarction or angina; acute renal failure, oliguria, hematuria, proteinuria, increases in BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, reduced urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath and languor; and, at an unknown frequency, Conn's syndrome, periorbital swelling, facial swelling, malaise, fever, nosebleed and peripheral edema.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, low-dose aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking it together with ACE inhibitors, lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendini

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199000568. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, adults take 1 to 2 tablets (275 to 550 mg) at a time, twice a day (every 12 hours). For acute gout, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 8 hours until the attack subsides. For skeletal muscle disorders, pain after surgery, pain after tooth extraction (having a tooth pulled), dysmenorrhea, tendinitis (inflammation of a tendon), and bursitis (inflammation of the lubricating sac), take 2 tablets (550 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 6 to 8 hours, and do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg). For migraine, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose); if necessary, 1 to 2 more tablets (275 to 550 mg) may be taken a day, and these are taken 30 minutes after the initial dose (the first dose). Do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as aspirin; patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe kidney disorder, or severe high blood pressure; patients who have had asthma, rhinitis (nasal inflammation), nasal polyps, urticaria, or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors); use for the treatment of pain occurring before or after coronary artery (heart artery) bypass surgery; and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, people who have had peptic ulcer, people who have had blood abnormalities, patients with a bleeding tendency, patients with liver disorder or a history of it, patients with kidney disorder or a history of it and patients with reduced renal blood flow, patients with cardiac dysfunction, high blood pressure, a history of hypersensitivity, bronchial asthma, systemic lupus erythematosus, or mixed connective tissue disease, and elderly people should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rarely, shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, bradycardia (slow pulse), cold sweat, swelling), PIE syndrome (pulmonary infiltration with eosinophilia: accompanied by fever, wheezing, cough, and sputum), urticaria, tinnitus (ringing in the ears), hearing impairment, visual impairment; occasionally, hypersensitivity symptoms such as rash and itching; rarely, hematemesis (vomiting of blood), gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation, abdominal distension, black stools, thirst, agranulocytosis, eosinophilia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic (red-blood-cell-destroying) anemia, and blood disorders such as reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), elevated GOT and GPT levels, jaundice, hepatitis, renal impairment (kidney disorder), glomerulonephritis (kidney inflammation), hematuria, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis (kidney inflammation), nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, proteinuria (urine containing protein), renal failure, aseptic meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness, etc.), photosensitivity, hair loss, redness (congested and reddened skin), necrolysis, erythema multiforme (red spots of various shapes), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), urticaria, epidermolysis bullosa, or drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, fixed drug eruption, palpitations, myasthenia (muscle weakness), congestive heart failure, eosinophilic pneumonia, anaphylactoid reaction, menstrual disorders, chills (feeling cold and shivering) and fever, vasculitis (inflammation of blood vessels), hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia; occasionally, gastric discomfort, stomach pain, abdominal pain (stomachache), nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, indigestion, heartburn, diarrhea, constipation, stomatitis (inflammation inside the mouth), drowsiness, cognitive impairment, eczema, sweating, purpura (purple spots), edema (swelling), and difficulty breathing.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics or naproxen derivatives, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with hydantoin antiepileptics, sulfonamides, sulfonylurea hypoglycemic agents, propranolol and other blockers, ACE inhibitors (such as captopril), loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics, probenecid, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (blood-clotting inhibitors) (such as warfarin), zidovudine, or new quinolone antibiotics (such as enoxacin).

Adults aged 15 years and older take 2 capsules per dose, 3 times a day 30 minutes after meals.

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.

  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.
  • If a severe skin adverse reaction such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis occurs, stop taking it and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine or have experienced such hypersensitivity, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants under 3 months of age, and patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure must not take this medicine.

Who should ask first

How to use the eye drops

Instill 2 to 3 drops 2 to 4 times a day. After instillation, discard the remaining solution and the container.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine must not use this medicine.
  • Before using this medicine, patients with considerable corneal damage should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If the symptoms do not improve after about 2 weeks of use, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • When it is given to a child, give it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Use this medicine only as eye drops.
  • When using it for the first time, discard the first 1 to 2 drops without instilling them.
  • Use this medicine only once after opening it.
  • Be careful, because if the tip of the container touches the eyelid or the eyelashes, the solution may become contaminated or cloudy from eye mucus, mold and the like.

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), fever and pain due to a cold, low back pain, dysmenorrhea, post-operative pain and ankylosing spondylitis, headache, toothache, muscle pain, neuralgia, acute gout, psoriatic arthritis, soft tissue injury (sprain, contusion), and non-articular rheumatic diseases (tendinitis, tenosynovitis, bursitis).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint diseas

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199804309. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 1/2 tablet to 1.5 tablets (200 to 600 mg) per dose 3 to 4 times a day, up to a maximum of 3200 mg a day. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30 to 40 mg per kg of body weight a day, divided into 3 to 4 doses; for mild to moderate pain or a cold, adults take 1/2 tablet to 1 tablet (200 to 400 mg) per dose 3 to 4 times a day. Children aged 11 to 14 years take 200 to 250 mg per dose, children aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg per dose, children aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg per dose, and children aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg per dose, orally 3 to 4 times a day. For children weighing less than 30 kg the daily amount must not exceed 500 mg, and it is preferable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. Do not take more than the recommended amount.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by patients who have or have had gastrointestinal ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding, by patients with severe blood abnormality, severe liver impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency or severe high blood pressure, by patients who have or have had bronchial asthma, by patients who have or have had hypersensitivity such as asthma, urticaria or an allergic reaction to aspirin or another non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesic (including COX-2 inhibitors), by patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, by pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, by patients taking high-dose methotrexate as anticancer therapy, or by patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the user has or has had blood abnormality, has a bleeding tendency, has or has had cirrhosis or liver impairment, has or has had renal impairment, has cardiac insufficiency or heart disease, high blood pressure, a history of hypersensitivity, systemic lupus erythematosus or mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, is elderly or a child, is a pregnant woman or a breast-feeding woman, or is taking low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke.
  • Without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist, do not take it for pain for 10 days or more (adults) or 5 days or more (children), and do not take it for fever for 3 days or more.

Possible side effects

  • If any of the following appears, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: symptoms of shock (heartburn, chills, difficulty breathing, fall in blood pressure); blood disorders such as decreased hematocrit, decreased hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time) and eosinophilia; peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, hematemesis, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, thirst, stomatitis, abdominal distension, oral ulcer, constipation and black stools; mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), photosensitivity reaction, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, exfoliative dermatitis and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis; hepatitis, jaundice, hepatic dysfunction such as increases in GOT, GPT and ALP, and liver impairment; hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reaction, asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purpura, rash, itching, asthma, bronchoconstriction, difficulty breathing or wheezing; visual disturbance such as a blind area of the visual field, hearing loss, tinnitus and abnormal taste; vertigo, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness; aseptic meningitis or meningitis (symptoms such as severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever or disturbance of consciousness); rise in blood pressure, palpitations, heart failure, myocardial infarction or angina; acute renal failure, oliguria, hematuria, proteinuria, increases in BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, reduced urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath and languor; and, at an unknown frequency, Conn's syndrome, periorbital swelling, facial swelling, malaise, fever, nosebleed and peripheral edema.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, low-dose aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking it together with ACE inhibitors, lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

This medicine is used for disinfection of the patient's skin before surgery or before insertion of a syringe needle or a catheter.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Topical medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for disinfection of the patient's skin before surgery or before insertion of a syringe needle or a

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201801818. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

Use this medicine in the following order. Remove the applicator from its packaging and hold it with the sponge facing downwards. Do not touch the sponge part of the applicator. Squeeze the applicator firmly only once so that the ampoule breaks and the solution comes out, and leave the broken ampoule inside the applicator. For the 26 mL product, squeeze the lever on the handle firmly, and for the other products squeeze both wings firmly. Do not squeeze or press the wings repeatedly in order to wet the sponge quickly. Press and release the sponge against the treatment area until the solution is visible on the skin, wetting the sponge and completely wetting the treatment area with the solution. For a dry surgical site (e.g. the abdomen or an arm), once the solution is visible on the skin, rub gently back and forth for 30 seconds to treat that area. For a moist surgical site (e.g. the groin fold), rub gently back and forth repeatedly for about 2 minutes. Let the area to which the solution has been applied dry completely in the air, and do not wipe the solution off. Discard the applicator after a single use, together with any remaining solution that was not used on the treatment area. It is not necessary to use the entire amount.

Precautions for use

  • People with hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine, isopropanol, or Yellow No. 5 and infants aged 2 months or younger should not use this medicine.
  • Do not use this medicine for disinfecting surgical instruments, or on nervous tissue (e.g., brain or spinal cord tissue), the eyes, ears, mouth, mucous membranes, genital mucous membranes, open wounds, or torn or damaged skin, or for general washing of the skin.
  • Before using this medicine, people with hypersensitivity to other medicines, people who have experienced allergic diseases such as asthma or who have a family history of them, people with hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine preparations, and people with a drug-hypersensitive constitution should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Use it externally only on intact skin.
  • Contact with the eyes may cause corneal damage, so be careful not to let it get into the eyes; if it does get in, rinse thoroughly with clean water immediately.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms (nausea, malaise, cold sweat, dizziness, a stifling feeling, difficulty breathing, redness, a sudden drop in blood pressure, urticaria, angioedema, etc.), occasionally rash, photosensitization, irritation, sensitization, erythema or inflammation, itching, dry and thinly peeling skin, local pain at the application site, or local skin reactions, or very rarely rash (e.g., erythematous, papular, or maculopapular), blisters, small blisters at the application site, a burning sensation of the skin, dermatitis, eczema, chemical burns in newborns, eye irritation, congestion, impaired vision, or eye damage occurs, stop using this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendinitis, acute gout, dysmenorrhea and bursitis, skeletal muscle disorders (sprain, contusion (bruise), trauma (wound), lumbosacral pain (low back pain)), postoperative pain (aches), migraine, and pain after tooth extraction (pulling out a tooth).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This drug is used for rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease), ankylosing spondylitis, tendini

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 199902599. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis, adults take 1 to 2 tablets (275 to 550 mg) at a time, twice a day (every 12 hours). For acute gout, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 8 hours until the attack subsides. For skeletal muscle disorders, pain after surgery, pain after tooth extraction (having a tooth pulled), dysmenorrhea, tendinitis (inflammation of a tendon), and bursitis (inflammation of the lubricating sac), take 2 tablets (550 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose), then take 1 tablet (275 mg) every 6 to 8 hours, and do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg). For migraine, take 3 tablets (825 mg) as the initial dose (the first dose); if necessary, 1 to 2 more tablets (275 to 550 mg) may be taken a day, and these are taken 30 minutes after the initial dose (the first dose). Do not let the total daily dose exceed 5 tablets (1,375 mg).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe renal disorder or severe high blood pressure, patients hypersensitive to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics such as aspirin, patients who have had asthma, rhinitis (nasal inflammation), nasal polyps, urticaria or an allergic reaction caused by aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors) or those who have experienced them, patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, and children aged 2 years or under must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women and women who may be pregnant, children, the elderly, those who have experienced peptic ulcer, those who have experienced blood abnormalities, patients with a tendency to bleed, patients with liver disorder or those who have experienced it, patients with renal disorder or those who have experienced it, and patients with cardiac dysfunction, high blood pressure, bronchial asthma, systemic lupus erythematosus or mixed connective tissue disease should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If an increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke, serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions that may be fatal such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcers, and perforation, rarely shock symptoms (difficulty breathing, a fall in blood pressure, bradycardia (a slow pulse), cold sweat, swelling), PIE syndrome (pulmonary infiltration with eosinophilia: accompanied by fever, wheezing, coughing, and phlegm), urticaria, occasionally hypersensitivity symptoms such as rash or itching, hematemesis (vomiting of blood), gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation, aseptic meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness), eczema, sweating, purpura (purple spots), photosensitivity, hair loss, redness (turning red from congestion), necrolysis, erythema multiforme (red spots of various shapes), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), urticaria, epidermolysis bullosa, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, fixed drug eruption, exfoliative dermatitis, or rarely blood disorders such as agranulocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic (red-blood-cell-destroying) anemia, or reduced platelet function (prolongation of bleeding time) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Occasionally stomach discomfort, stomach pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, indigestion, heartburn, diarrhea, constipation, or stomatitis (inflammation inside the mouth), and rarely abdominal bloating, black stools, dry mouth, elevated GOT and GPT values, jaundice, hepatitis, kidney disorder, nephritis, hematuria, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, proteinuria (urine containing protein), renal failure, ringing in the ears, hearing impairment, visual impairment, swelling, difficulty breathing, palpitations (a pounding heart), myasthenia (muscle weakness), congestive heart failure, eosinophilic pneumonia, anaphylactoid reactions, menstrual disorders, chills (feeling cold and shivering) and fever, vasculitis, high blood sugar, or low blood sugar may occur.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics or naproxen derivatives, aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with hydantoin antiepileptics, sulfonamides, sulfonylurea hypoglycemic agents, propranolol and other blockers, ACE inhibitors (such as captopril), loop diuretics and thiazide diuretics, probenecid, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (blood-clotting inhibitors) (such as warfarin), zidovudine, or new quinolone antibiotics (such as enoxacin).

At a glance

Category

How it works

This medicine is used for disinfection inside the mouth, pharyngitis, laryngitis, stomatitis, disinfection after tooth e

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201600528. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

Spray and apply an appropriate amount several times in 1 day.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with thyroid dysfunction, and children under 6 years of age must not use this medicine, and it must not be used during radioactive iodine therapy or before and after such therapy.
  • Before using this medicine, patients with severe sores in the mouth, women who are pregnant, may be pregnant, or are breastfeeding, and patients who are hypersensitive to propylene glycol or have been in the past should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Use it for the mouth only.
  • In the case of an oral wound such as after a tooth extraction, avoid vigorous rinsing until the blood has clotted and the bleeding has stopped.
  • If the symptoms do not improve or become worse, consult a doctor.
  • It may affect thyroid diagnosis using scintigraphy.
  • Allow an interval of 4 weeks or more between the use of this medicine and a scintigraphy examination.
  • Excessive use of this medicine as a disinfectant may cause iodine toxicity.
  • If it gets on clothing, it washes out easily with water if rinsed immediately.
  • If a large amount accidentally enters the mouth or it gets into the eyes, act immediately.
  • Keep it from coming into contact with jewelry (especially items containing silver).
  • When it is used by children, have them use it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.

Possible side effects

  • If pneumonia, occasionally irritation of the mouth and throat or nausea, rarely erosion of the oral mucosa, sores in the mouth, contact dermatitis or discomfort, or very rarely angioedema occur, stop using this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200-600 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. Up to a maximum of 3,200 mg a day may be taken. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30 to 40 mg per kg of body weight per dose, in 3 to 4 divided doses a day. For mild to moderate pain and for colds, adults take 200 to 400 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. The dose may be increased or decreased as appropriate according to age and symptoms. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years take 200 to 250 mg (10 to 12.5 mL) per dose, those aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg (7.5 to 10 mL) per dose, those aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg (5 to 7.5 mL) per dose, and those aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg (2.5 to 5 mL) per dose, 3 to 4 times a day, and it is advisable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years may take up to 1,000 mg (50 mL) a day, those aged 7 to 10 years up to 800 mg (40 mL), those aged 3 to 6 years up to 600 mg (30 mL), and those aged 1 to 2 years up to 400 mg (20 mL).

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

  • Before taking this medicine, patients with blood abnormalities or a bleeding tendency, patients with liver cirrhosis, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, heart disease, high blood pressure, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people, children under 2 years of age, pregnant women, and patients with chickenpox should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • When taking it for a cold, take it for no more than 5 days as a rule, and without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist do not take it for pain for 10 days or more (adults) or 5 days or more (children), and do not take it for fever for 3 days or more.

Category

How it works

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201904193. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200 to 600 mg at a time, 3 to 4 times a day, up to a maximum of 3200 mg per day. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30 to 40 mg per kg of body weight per day, divided into 3 to 4 doses. For mild to moderate pain and colds, adults take 200 to 400 mg at a time, children aged 11 to 14 years take 200 to 250 mg (10 to 13 mL) at a time, children aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg (8 to 10 mL) at a time, children aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg (5 to 8 mL) at a time, and children aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg (3 to 5 mL) at a time, 3 to 4 times a day. For children weighing less than 30 kg, the daily dose must not exceed 500 mg (25 mL), and it is preferable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach.

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, patients with gastrointestinal ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding or a history of it, patients with severe blood disorders, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure or bronchial asthma or a history of it, patients with hypersensitivity such as asthma, urticaria or allergic reactions to aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors) or a history of it, patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG), pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, and patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as anticancer therapy must not take this medicine.

  • If any of the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: shock symptoms (chest distress (heartburn), chills, difficulty breathing, a drop in blood pressure, etc.); blood disorders such as decreased hematocrit, decreased hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), and eosinophilia; peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, hematemesis (vomiting of blood), Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, thirst, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, mouth ulcers, constipation, black stools; skin-mucosa-eye syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), photosensitivity reactions, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome), angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash; hepatitis, jaundice, abnormal liver function such as elevated GOT, GPT and ALP, liver disorder; hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reactions, asthma attacks, hives, eczema, purpura (purple spots), rash, itching, asthma, bronchoconstriction, difficulty breathing or wheezing; visual disturbances such as scotoma (an area of vision loss), hearing loss (deafness), ringing in the ears, taste disturbance, vertigo, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness, aseptic meningitis or meningitis (symptoms such as severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever, or disturbance of consciousness); a drop in blood pressure, a rise in blood pressure, palpitations (pounding heart), heart failure, myocardial infarction or angina; acute renal failure, oliguria (decreased urination), blood in the urine, protein in the urine, elevated BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath, lethargy, periorbital edema (swelling around the eyes), facial edema (swelling of the face), malaise, fever, nosebleed, swelling, and peripheral edema.

Interactions

  • Do not take it together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics or with high-dose methotrexate used in cancer chemotherapy.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking it together with low-dose aspirin, ACE inhibitors, lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

How to apply it

For nebulization therapy using a face mask, mouthpiece, or tracheostomy, nebulize 1 to 10 mL every 2 to 6 hours. The recommended amount is 3 to 5 mL nebulized 3 to 4 times a day. Nebulization therapy using a mist tent or an inhalation device (Croupette) is a method needed in special cases and is used on an individual basis according to the patient's personal needs and the convenience of the administration method. This method of administration requires a large volume of solution, and sometimes up to about 300 mL may be required for a single treatment. The recommended amount should be a volume that can maintain a very dense, fog-like state inside the tent or inhalation device throughout the treatment period. Intermittent or continuous long-term administration is desirable. For direct instillation, administer 1 to 2 mL every hour. For the routine treatment of patients who have had a tracheostomy, administer 1 to 2 mL through the tracheostomy every 1 to 4 hours. When administering directly to a specific part of the bronchial tree of the lung by inserting a small plastic catheter into the trachea under local anesthesia and a direct incision, administer 2 to 5 mL every 1 to 4 hours using a syringe connected to the catheter. For diagnostic bronchography, administer 1 to 2 mL 2 to 3 times before performing the bronchography, by nebulization or by instillation into the bronchi.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine should not use it.
  • Before using this medicine, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, patients with bronchial asthma or accompanying respiratory insufficiency, elderly people, and children should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • It is not used as an injection or as eye drops.
  • After nebulization therapy the face mask may stick to the face, but it comes off easily when washed with water.

Possible side effects

  • A slight odor (a sulfurous smell), occasionally nausea, vomiting and loss of appetite, and rarely bloody sputum, chills, fever, runny nose, stomatitis, drowsiness, a feeling of pressure in the chest, and irritation of the trachea and bronchi may occur.

Interactions

  • When it is necessary to use this medicine together with an antibiotic, inhale them separately, or give the antibiotic by injection or orally.

Oral medicine (MFDS 201903800)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201903800. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, cough, phlegm, chills (feeling cold and shivering), fever, headache, joint pain, muscle pain).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, co

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201903800. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults aged 15 years and older take 2 capsules per dose, 3 times a day 30 minutes after meals.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious and potentially fatal skin reactions such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.
  • If a severe skin adverse reaction such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis occurs, stop taking it and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine or have experienced such hypersensitivity, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants under 3 months of age, and patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, infants and children under 15 years of age who have or are suspected of having a chickenpox or influenza infection, infants and young children under 2 years of age, women who are pregnant or may be pregnant, breastfeeding women, the elderly, people with a weak body, people with an allergic constitution, people who have experienced allergic symptoms (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.), and patients with liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.), difficulty urinating, high fever, stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort or stomach pain, ulcer or bleeding problems, smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough that lasts more than 1 week or recurs, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever and rash or a persistent headache should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • Do not take it continuously over a long period.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking it 5 to 6 times, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If rash, redness, itching, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling, and chest tightness immediately after taking the medicine, along with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (accompanied by high fever, with severe symptoms such as rash and redness and blistering like burns appearing on the skin all over the body and on the mucous membranes of the mouth or eyes), acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, asthma, general fatigue, jaundice, interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, and fever), or ischemic colitis (sudden abdominal pain, rectal bleeding) occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If symptoms of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (sudden severe headache, thunderclap headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance, etc.) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other products containing acetaminophen, MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussive expectorants, other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • People who are within 2 weeks of having stopped taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) must not take this medicine.
  • If you take it together with diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants or alcohol, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold, such as sore throat, chills with feeling cold and shivering, fever, headache, joint pain, and muscle pain.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used to relieve the various symptoms of a cold, such as sore throat, chills with feeling cold and shive

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202303159. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

People aged 15 years and over and adults take 1 tablet per dose, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after a meal.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported, and if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily amount of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products that contain acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine or have been in the past, people who have experienced asthma when taking this medicine or its ingredients, other antipyretic analgesics, or cold remedies, infants under 3 months of age and children under 2 years of age, women after 30 weeks of pregnancy, and patients with genetic problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if you have an allergic constitution or have experienced allergic symptoms to medicines such as fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, or itching; if the user is an infant or a child under 15 years of age who has or is suspected of having chickenpox or influenza; if you are pregnant, may be pregnant, or are breastfeeding; if the user is a child under 2 years of age for whom it is strictly necessary; if you are frail or have a high fever; if you have liver disease, kidney disease, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, or gastroduodenal ulcer; if you have persistent or recurring stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain, or have ulcer or bleeding problems; or if you are hypersensitive to Yellow No. 4 (tartrazine) or have been in the past.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after taking 5 to 6 doses, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.

Possible side effects

  • If rash, redness with congestion and reddening, itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, or dizziness occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Rarely, if shock (anaphylaxis), in which urticaria, swelling, and chest tightness appear right after taking the medicine together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing, or mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), asthma, general languor, liver dysfunction such as jaundice, or interstitial pneumonia occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • While taking this medicine, do not take antitussives and expectorants, other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives or oral medicines containing an antihistamine.
  • People who are taking an MAO inhibitor used for the treatment of depression, Parkinson's disease and the like, or who are within 2 weeks of stopping one, should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, people who are being given a diabetes medicine, a gout medicine, an arthritis medicine, an anticoagulant, a steroid or the like should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Patients who are being given a barbiturate, a tricyclic antidepressant or alcohol should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.

payloads.summary: This medicine is used for chronic constipation, constipation in infants, young children, and children, and constipation
payloads.content:

Oral medicine (MFDS 201706514)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201706514. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used for chronic constipation, constipation in infants, young children, and children, and constipation after childbirth.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for chronic constipation, constipation in infants, young children, and children, and constipation

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201706514. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For chronic constipation, adults take 15 to 30 mL a day before breakfast for the first 2 to 3 days, and thereafter continue with 10 to 15 mL a day. In severe cases up to 45 mL may be taken. Children (7 to 14 years) take 15 mL a day for the first 2 to 3 days and thereafter continue with 10 mL a day. Young children (1 to 6 years) take 5 to 10 mL a day, and infants (under 12 months) take 5 mL a day.

Precautions for use

  • Patients hypersensitive to this medicine, patients with inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease), gastrointestinal obstruction, abdominal pain of unknown cause, a low-galactose diet (galactosemia), or gastrointestinal perforation or a risk of it, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, infants, young children and children, the elderly, and patients with diabetes, fructose intolerance, fluid and electrolyte imbalance, acute gastritis or chronic constipation should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If loose stools or diarrhea occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Belching, cramping abdominal discomfort, and occasionally borborygmi, abdominal bloating, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea, and vomiting may occur.

Interactions

  • Patients who take α-glucosidase inhibitors such as acarbose, broad-spectrum antibiotics, diuretics, corticosteroids, amphotericin B, cardiac glycosides, or antacids should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

payloads.content:

Oral medicine (MFDS 198701129)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 198701129. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used for difficulty in expectoration in diseases such as acute and chronic bronchitis, bronchial asthma, laryngitis, sinusitis, and cystic fibrosis.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for difficulty in expectoration in diseases such as acute and chronic bronchitis, bronchial asthma

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 198701129. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

For an acute disease, adults take 1 sachet (200 mg) per dose 3 times a day, children aged 6 to 14 years take 1 sachet (200 mg) per dose twice a day, and children aged 2 to 5 years take 1/2 sachet (100 mg) per dose 3 times a day, in each case with a small amount of water. For a chronic disease, adults take 1 sachet (200 mg) per dose twice a day, and children aged 6 to 14 years take 1/2 sachet (100 mg) per dose 3 times a day, in each case with a small amount of water. For cystic fibrosis, people aged 6 years and over take 1 sachet (200 mg) per dose 3 times a day, and children aged 2 to 5 years take 1/2 sachet (100 mg) per dose 4 times a day, in each case with a small amount of water.

Warning

  • Because this medicine contains aspartame, which is metabolized to phenylalanine in the body, patients with phenylketonuria who need to restrict phenylalanine intake should not take it.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by patients with gastric or duodenal ulcer, or by infants under 2 years of age.
  • Before taking this medicine, a pregnant woman or a woman who may be pregnant and a breast-feeding woman should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If, rarely, nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, heartburn, diarrhea, urticaria, itching, rash, headache, tinnitus, bronchospasm (especially in asthma patients), tachycardia, hypertension, and very rarely anaphylaxis or the like appear, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • When taking it together with oral antibiotics (amoxicillin, cefuroxime, doxycycline, erythromycin, thiamphenicol), leave an interval of at least 2 hours.
  • Avoid adding other medicines to the solution of this medicine.

This medicine is used for the temporary relief of a burning sensation, irritation, and discomfort caused by dryness of the eyes or by wind and sun, and for the prevention of eye irritation.

At a glance

How it works

This medicine is used for the temporary relief of a burning sensation, irritation, and discomfort caused by dryness of t

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 200904757. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to use the eye drops

When needed, instill 1 to 2 drops into the affected eye. In the case of single-use containers, discard the remaining solution and the container immediately after instillation.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine must not use this medicine.
  • Before using this medicine, patients with severe eye pain and people who have so far experienced allergic symptoms from eye drops (e.g. redness of the eyes, itching, swelling, rash, congestion causing reddening, etc.) should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • When it is used in children, use it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Use this medicine for ophthalmic instillation only.
  • Do not use it as a wetting solution for soft contact lenses or while wearing soft contact lenses.
  • If the tip of the container touches the eyelid or eyelashes, the solution may become contaminated or cloudy because of eye discharge or mold, so be careful, and do not use it if it has become cloudy.
  • To prevent contamination, avoid sharing it with others as far as possible.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after using it for 3 days, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If itching, swelling, eye pain, changes in the field of vision, or persistent redness or a feeling of irritation of the eye occurs, or if a person wearing hard contact lenses has heavy discharge such as eye mucus and, rarely, the lenses become cloudy, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

This medicine is used for the early treatment of recurrent herpes labialis (cold sores).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Topical medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for the early treatment of recurrent herpes labialis (cold sores).

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202000951. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

Adults use an appropriate amount, enough to cover the affected area (the diseased part) fully to its edge, 5 times a day for 5 days. Start the treatment as soon as possible, right when the first symptoms and signs appear.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be used by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by breast-feeding women, by children under 18 years of age, by patients with a skin infection (tuberculosis, syphilis, candidiasis, tinea, herpes zoster, chickenpox, vaccinia, scabies, pubic lice), by patients whose immune system is seriously impaired (bone marrow transplant patients, AIDS patients), by patients with eczematous otitis externa with perforation of the eardrum, ulcer (except Behcet's disease), a burn or frostbite of deep second degree or worse, perioral dermatitis, acne vulgaris or rosacea, or by patients who have or have had myocardial infarction.
  • Before using this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the user is a pregnant woman or a woman who may be pregnant, is elderly, or has or has had hypersensitivity to propylene glycol.
  • Do not use it in the eyes, the nose, the mouth or the genitals.
  • Use it only on herpes labialis (cold sores) on the lips or around the mouth.
  • Follow the prescribed directions and amounts.
  • Do not use this medicine as a base for diluting it or for mixing other medicines.

Possible side effects

  • If a feeling of dryness or peeling of the skin, which are common, a temporary burning sensation (a hot feeling) or numbness, which occur occasionally, or, rarely, erythema (red spots), pigmentation or the symptoms and signs of inflammation occurs, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Because of systemic absorption, reversible suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, Cushing's syndrome, hyperglycemia, diabetes and visual disturbance may occur.

Children aged 12 years and older and adults take 0.5–1 g (1/2–1 measuring spoon) once a day, and children aged 3 months and older but under 12 years take 0.5 g (1/2 measuring spoon) once a day.It may be taken mixed with food (such as porridge).

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, renal failure, renal osteodystrophy, hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, hyperphosphatemia, primary hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, chronic plasmacytoma, bone metastases, urinary tract stones, osteoporosis in an immobilized state, long-term immobilization with hypercalciuria or hypercalcemia, or hypothyroidism, and patients being treated with calcitriol or other vitamin D metabolites must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, pregnant women and breastfeeding women and patients with kidney stones, arteriosclerosis, or heart disease should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • If, rarely, hypersensitivity reactions, itching, rash, urticaria, abdominal pain, flatulence, constipation, diarrhea, bloating, nausea or vomiting occur, very rarely allergic reactions (facial edema, angioneurotic edema) occur, or uncommonly hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria or hyperphosphatemia occurs, stop taking the medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take this medicine together with calcitriol or other vitamin D preparations.

  • Oxalic acid (spinach, rhubarb) and phytic acid (whole-grain cereals) can inhibit the absorption of calcium, so take this medicine 2 hours after eating such foods.

Who should ask first

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over and adults take 2 tablets at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals; those aged 7 years and over but under 15 years take 1 tablet at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or other signs of a hypersensitivity reaction appear after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.

  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products containing acetaminophen.
  • If severe skin adverse reactions such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis occur, stop taking it and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or a history of it, people who have had an asthma attack when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, infants (newborns) under 3 months of age, patients with severe or uncontrolled high blood pressure, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist in the following cases: patients with hypersensitivity to Yellow No. 5 or a history of it; people who have had allergies caused by medicines; children 3 months of age and older but under 2 years of age; infants and children under 15 years of age who are infected with or suspected of having chickenpox or influenza; people with an allergic constitution; people with liver, kidney, heart, or thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.), or difficulty urinating (passing urine); elderly people (the aged); people who are physically weak or have a high fever; people with persistent or recurring stomach problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain, or with ulcers or bleeding problems; women who are pregnant or may be pregnant; breastfeeding women; and symptoms such as smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough with excessive phlegm, a cough lasting 1 week or longer or recurring, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever and rash or a persistent headache.
  • Follow the specified dosage and administration carefully.
  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • When it is given to children, give it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • If symptoms do not improve after taking it 5 to 6 times, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness (congested and reddened skin), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema (swelling), difficulty urinating (passing urine), persistent or severe thirst, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling, or chest tightness immediately after taking it, together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome: accompanied by high fever, with severe symptoms such as rash and redness and burn-like blistering), acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (a severe skin adverse reaction with fever, erythema, and numerous small pustules), asthma, generalized lassitude, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes turn yellow), interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.), symptoms of ischemic colitis related to the pseudoephedrine component (sudden abdominal pain, rectal bleeding), or posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (sudden severe headache, thunderclap headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance, etc.) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussives and expectorants (cough and phlegm medicines), other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis [nasal inflammation], motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).People who stopped taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) within the past 2 weeks must not take this medicine.People receiving other medicines such as barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants and alcohol, antidiabetic medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, or steroids should consult a doctor or pharmacist.Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.
