  • If rash, redness, itching, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema, difficulty urinating, thirst (persistent or severe), dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, high anion gap metabolic acidosis, rarely shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling, or chest tightness immediately after taking it, together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat, and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (accompanied by high fever, with severe symptoms such as rash and redness and burn-like blistering appearing on the skin over the whole body, the mouth, or the mucous membranes of the eyes), asthma, generalized lassitude, jaundice, interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by cough, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, and fever), or symptoms of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (sudden severe headache, thunderclap headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinson drugs, etc.), antitussive-expectorants, other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines), or preparations containing diphenhydramine.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.
  • If taken together with diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol or flucloxacillin, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Category

How it works

This medicine is used for rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis (degenerative joint diseas

Why this one

Who should ask first

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200-600 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. Up to a maximum of 3,200 mg a day may be taken. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30 to 40 mg per kg of body weight per dose, in 3 to 4 divided doses a day. For mild to moderate pain and for colds, adults take 200 to 400 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. The dose may be increased or decreased as appropriate according to age and symptoms. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years take 200 to 250 mg (10 to 12.5 mL) per dose, those aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg (7.5 to 10 mL) per dose, those aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg (5 to 7.5 mL) per dose, and those aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg (2.5 to 5 mL) per dose, 3 to 4 times a day, and it is advisable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years may take up to 1,000 mg (50 mL) a day, those aged 7 to 10 years up to 800 mg (40 mL), those aged 3 to 6 years up to 600 mg (30 mL), and those aged 1 to 2 years up to 400 mg (20 mL).

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, severe blood abnormalities, severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma, patients who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, breastfeeding women, patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Do not take more than the recommended dose.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with blood abnormalities or a bleeding tendency, patients with liver cirrhosis, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, heart disease, high blood pressure, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people, children under 2 years of age, pregnant women, and patients with chickenpox should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • When taking it for a cold, take it for no more than 5 days as a rule, and without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist do not take it for pain for 10 days or more (adults) or 5 days or more (children), and do not take it for fever for 3 days or more.

  • If shock (difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, etc.), decreased hematocrit, decreased hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, decreased platelet function, or blood disorders such as eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation (a hole forming), ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, vomiting of blood, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal bloating, oral ulcer, constipation, black stools, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, exfoliative dermatitis, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, hepatitis, jaundice, liver function abnormalities, hepatic impairment, hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reaction, asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purple spots, visual disturbance, deafness, ringing in the ears, taste disturbance, dizziness, drowsiness, lightheadedness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness, aseptic meningitis or meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever or disturbance of consciousness), acute renal failure, decreased urination, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN or blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and accompanying shortness of breath, listlessness, Kounis syndrome of unknown frequency, swelling around the eyes, facial swelling, malaise, fever, nosebleed, swelling, or peripheral edema occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy should not take this medicine, and do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics.
  • Before taking this medicine, people taking low-dose aspirin or ACE inhibitors and patients taking lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, low-dose methotrexate, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

This medicine is used for difficulty in expectorating sputum in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pulmonary tuberculosis, emphysema, upper respiratory tract inflammation (pharyngitis and laryngitis), lung abscess, pneumonia, cystic fibrosis and postoperative pulmonary complications, and for the preparation and aftercare of bronchography, bronchoscopy, lung cancer cytology and tracheostomy.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Topical medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for difficulty in expectorating sputum in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pu

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201903112. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

For nebulization therapy using a face mask, mouthpiece, or tracheostomy, nebulize 1 to 10 mL every 2 to 6 hours. The recommended amount is 3 to 5 mL nebulized 3 to 4 times a day. Nebulization therapy using a mist tent or an inhalation device (Croupette) is a method needed in special cases and is used on an individual basis according to the patient's personal needs and the convenience of the administration method. This method of administration requires a large volume of solution, and sometimes up to about 300 mL may be required for a single treatment. The recommended amount should be a volume that can maintain a very dense, fog-like state inside the tent or inhalation device throughout the treatment period. Intermittent or continuous long-term administration is desirable. For direct instillation, administer 1 to 2 mL every hour. For the routine treatment of patients who have had a tracheostomy, administer 1 to 2 mL through the tracheostomy every 1 to 4 hours. When administering directly to a specific part of the bronchial tree of the lung by inserting a small plastic catheter into the trachea under local anesthesia and a direct incision, administer 2 to 5 mL every 1 to 4 hours using a syringe connected to the catheter. For diagnostic bronchography, administer 1 to 2 mL 2 to 3 times before performing the bronchography, by nebulization or by instillation into the bronchi.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine should not use it.
  • Before using this medicine, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, patients with bronchial asthma or accompanying respiratory insufficiency, elderly people, and children should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • It is not used as an injection or as eye drops.
  • After nebulization therapy the face mask may stick to the face, but it comes off easily when washed with water.

Possible side effects

  • A slight odor (a sulfurous smell), occasionally nausea, vomiting and loss of appetite, and rarely bloody sputum, chills, fever, runny nose, stomatitis, drowsiness, a feeling of pressure in the chest, and irritation of the trachea and bronchi may occur.

Interactions

  • When it is necessary to use this medicine together with an antibiotic, inhale them separately, or give the antibiotic by injection or orally.

  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • When giving it to a child, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.
  • If the symptoms do not improve after taking it 5 to 6 times, consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • If rash and redness (congested and reddened skin), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema (swelling), difficulty urinating (passing urine), persistent or severe thirst, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, shock symptoms (urticaria, swelling and tightness in the chest immediately after taking it, together with a pale complexion, cold hands and feet, cold sweats and difficulty breathing), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome: severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, such as rash and redness and blisters like burns), asthma, listlessness of the whole body, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes taking on a yellow color) or interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, breathlessness, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.) occurs, stop taking the medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian drugs, etc.), antitussives and expectorants (cough and phlegm medicines), other cold medicines, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis [nasal inflammation], motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • People who are receiving other drugs such as barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants and alcohol, diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, or steroids should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Category

How it works

This medicine is used for fever and pain due to colds, headache, neuralgia, muscle pain, menstrual pain, and pain from s

Why this one

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Children aged 12 years and under take the following recommended 1-time dose every 4 to 6 hours as needed. For the recommended 1-time dose by age group, refer to the approved labeling. Take the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible period, and do not take it more than 5 times a day (75 mg/kg). If the body weight is known, it is more appropriate to take a dose based on body weight (10 to 15 mg/kg).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported, and if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily amount of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products that contain acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood disorders, liver disorder, kidney disorder, or reduced cardiac function, and patients with aspirin-induced asthma or a history of it must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, children under 2 years of age, patients with a bleeding tendency, patients with or a history of liver disorder, kidney disorder, or blood disorders, those with a history of peptic ulcer, patients with bronchial asthma or abnormal cardiac function, those who have experienced hypersensitivity, elderly people, pregnant women, and nursing mothers should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If pain or fever persists or worsens, or if new symptoms appear, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Without instructions from a doctor or pharmacist, adults must not take it for pain for 10 days or longer and children must not take it for 5 days or longer, and it must not be taken for fever for 3 days or longer.
  • Children and elderly people should take the minimum necessary amount and watch for adverse reactions.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms such as difficulty breathing, reddening of the whole body, angioedema, or urticaria, or an asthma attack, thrombocytopenia, granulocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, methemoglobinemia, decreased platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), or hypersensitivity symptoms such as cyanosis, facial swelling, sweating, or low blood pressure, or nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, gastrointestinal bleeding, peptic ulcer, perforation, rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), elevated AST, elevated ALT, or fixed drug eruption occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • People who have taken barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol should not take this medicine.
  • Do not take it together with other anti-inflammatory analgesics.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients on long-term warfarin and patients taking lithium or thiazide diuretics should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis have been reported; if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.

  • Do not take this medicine together with barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol.
  • People who are being given other medicines such as warfarin or flucloxacillin should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Avoid taking it together with other anti-inflammatory analgesics.

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

Spray this medicine into each nostril every 2 to 3 hours as needed. The number of sprays varies according to age. Insert the nozzle into the nostril and point its tip slightly backwards. Press the pump firmly to activate the spray, spray the specified amount into both nostrils, then tilt your head to the right for 10 seconds and then to the left for 10 seconds. After that, hold your nose with your hand to close the nostrils and bend your head forward for 10 seconds. Infants may be given 1 spray, those aged 1 month to 12 months 1 to 2 sprays, those aged 1 to 2 years 1 to 3 sprays, those aged 2 to 5 years 1 to 4 sprays, those aged 5 to 8 years 1 to 5 sprays, those aged 8 to 12 years 1 to 6 sprays, and adults 1 to 8 sprays.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine or to benzalkonium chloride must not use this medicine.

  • Use this medicine only as a nasal preparation, that is, a medicine applied inside the nose.
  • One product should be used by only one person.
  • To keep the solution from running down into the larynx or pharynx, use it while lying on your side at an angle or while standing with your head tilted.

Possible side effects

  • This medicine contains benzalkonium chloride, so it may cause bronchospasm.

Those 8 years and older and adults take 2 tablets at a time, twice a day.

unknown frequency, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, rash, urticaria, itching, purpura, rarely asthma attacks, eczema, anaphylactic reactions, photosensitivity reactions, jaundice, elevated ALT, elevated AST, elevated ALP, abnormal liver function, hepatitis, occasionally rhinitis, bronchospasm, rarely a risk of acute pneumonia in patients with heart failure, visual impairment such as loss of vision in front of the eyes and scotoma, hearing loss, tinnitus, taste disturbance, fatigue, drowsiness, headache, dizziness, occasionally anxiety, restlessness, confusion, depression, rarely aseptic meningitis, a drop in blood pressure, a rise in blood pressure, palpitations, acute renal failure, oliguria (decreased urine), or hematuria, as well as elevated urinary protein (protein contained in the urine), BUN, or blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, acute pulmonary edema, peripheral edema, fluid retention, reduced fertility in women, periorbital edema, very rarely malaise, fever, nosebleeds, or worsening of inflammation occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

This medicine is used for difficulty in expectorating sputum in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pulmonary tuberculosis, emphysema, upper respiratory tract inflammation (pharyngitis and laryngitis), lung abscess, pneumonia, cystic fibrosis and postoperative pulmonary complications, and for the preparation and aftercare of bronchography, bronchoscopy, lung cancer cytology and tracheostomy.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Topical medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for difficulty in expectorating sputum in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pu

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201903112. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

For nebulization therapy using a face mask, mouthpiece, or tracheostomy, nebulize 1 to 10 mL every 2 to 6 hours. The recommended amount is 3 to 5 mL nebulized 3 to 4 times a day. Nebulization therapy using a mist tent or an inhalation device (Croupette) is a method needed in special cases and is used on an individual basis according to the patient's personal needs and the convenience of the administration method. This method of administration requires a large volume of solution, and sometimes up to about 300 mL may be required for a single treatment. The recommended amount should be a volume that can maintain a very dense, fog-like state inside the tent or inhalation device throughout the treatment period. Intermittent or continuous long-term administration is desirable. For direct instillation, administer 1 to 2 mL every hour. For the routine treatment of patients who have had a tracheostomy, administer 1 to 2 mL through the tracheostomy every 1 to 4 hours. When administering directly to a specific part of the bronchial tree of the lung by inserting a small plastic catheter into the trachea under local anesthesia and a direct incision, administer 2 to 5 mL every 1 to 4 hours using a syringe connected to the catheter. For diagnostic bronchography, administer 1 to 2 mL 2 to 3 times before performing the bronchography, by nebulization or by instillation into the bronchi.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine should not use it.
  • Before using this medicine, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, patients with bronchial asthma or accompanying respiratory insufficiency, elderly people, and children should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • It is not used as an injection or as eye drops.
  • After nebulization therapy the face mask may stick to the face, but it comes off easily when washed with water.

Possible side effects

  • A slight odor (a sulfurous smell), occasionally nausea, vomiting and loss of appetite, and rarely bloody sputum, chills, fever, runny nose, stomatitis, drowsiness, a feeling of pressure in the chest, and irritation of the trachea and bronchi may occur.

Interactions

  • When it is necessary to use this medicine together with an antibiotic, inhale them separately, or give the antibiotic by injection or orally.

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious and potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with peptic ulcer, severe blood abnormalities, severe liver impairment, severe kidney impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency, or severe hypertension, patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, patients with bronchial asthma or those who have experienced it, those with asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions to aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics (including COX-2 inhibitors) or those who have experienced them, and patients being treated for pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery must not take this medicine.Those who have experienced peptic ulcer, those with blood abnormalities or who have experienced them, patients with a tendency to bleed, patients with liver impairment or kidney impairment or those who have experienced them, patients with cardiac insufficiency or hypertension, those who have experienced hypersensitivity, patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people and children, and patients with gastric cancer should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking it.

  • If the following occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rarely, shock symptoms (chest discomfort, chills, difficulty breathing, drop in blood pressure, etc.), aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), and blood disorders such as eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) or toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, induction of asthma attacks, urticaria, eczema, purpura; occasionally, rash, itching, visual disturbances such as neglect and scotoma, aseptic meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness, etc.), acute renal failure, oliguria (decreased urine), hematuria, proteinuria, and elevated BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia.Occasionally, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, and gastric discomfort; very rarely, thirst, stomatitis, abdominal distension, and constipation; rarely, jaundice, elevated GOT, GPT, and AL-P, hearing loss, tinnitus, taste disturbance, drop in blood pressure, rise in blood pressure, palpitations, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and accompanying shortness of breath, and lassitude; occasionally, periorbital edema; and very rarely, malaise, fever, and nosebleed may occur.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics or high-dose methotrexate.
  • If you take it together with glucocorticoids, alcohol, digoxin, phenytoin, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, sulfonylureas, diuretics, antihypertensives, ACE inhibitors, furosemide, aspirin, lithium, low-dose methotrexate, or coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), consult a doctor or pharmacist.

This medicine is used as an adjunct in the treatment of chronic polyarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, arthropathy, ankylosing spondylitis, painful swelling or inflammation after trauma and surgery, and infections accompanied by inflammation, pain, and fever.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used as an adjunct in the treatment of chronic polyarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, arthropathy, ankylo

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201702324. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults take 1 capsule (300 mg) at a time, 2 to 4 times a day. However, do not exceed 4 capsules (1,200 mg) a day.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more alcoholic drinks every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or other antipyretic analgesics.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious, potentially fatal cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, patients with or a history of gastrointestinal ulcer, patients with bleeding in the gastrointestinal tract, the cerebral blood vessels, or other sites, severe blood disorders, severe liver disorder, severe kidney disorder, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma or a history of it, those who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or an allergic reaction to aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients being treated for pain before or after coronary artery (heart artery) bypass graft surgery (CABG), pregnant women at 6 months of pregnancy or later, nursing mothers, patients with inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, and those who have experienced gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation from previous treatment with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with or a history of blood disorders, patients with a bleeding tendency, patients with or a history of liver disorder or kidney disorder, patients with fluid retention (accumulation of body fluid) or heart failure, patients with high blood pressure, those who have experienced hypersensitivity, patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), elderly people, children aged 6 years and older, patients with stomach cancer or alcoholism, pregnant women in early or mid pregnancy and women who may be pregnant, patients with ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease, or risk factors for cardiovascular disease (e.g., high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking), patients with hepatic porphyria, patients who have had major surgery that caused blood loss, patients with a blood coagulation disorder or who are receiving anticoagulants, and those who have experienced hypersensitivity or an allergic reaction to Yellow No. 5 should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Considering the importance of the drug treatment, either stop breastfeeding or stop taking the drug.
  • Dizziness or fatigue may occur after taking this medicine, so be careful when driving or operating machinery.
  • When it is taken for a long period for an acute illness, in principle this should be limited to within 5 days.

Possible side effects

  • If the following occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist: rarely shock (chest discomfort, chills, difficulty breathing, lowered blood pressure, etc.); rarely blood disorders such as aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, agranulocytosis, pancytopenia, thrombocytopenia, decreased platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), and eosinophilia; indigestion, abdominal distension, heartburn, upper abdominal pain, diarrhea or constipation; occasionally loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or stomach discomfort; rarely esophagitis, esophageal stricture, worsening of diverticula, nonspecific hemorrhagic colitis, ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, bloody stools, gastritis, or pancreatitis; very rarely thirst, stomatitis, erythema multiforme, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), or hair loss; occasionally angioedema; rarely Stevens-Johnson syndrome (mucocutaneous ocular syndrome) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome); drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency; occasionally rash, urticaria, itching, or purpura; rarely induction of an asthma attack, eczema, anaphylactic reactions, or photosensitivity reactions; rarely jaundice, elevated ALT, elevated AST, elevated ALP, abnormal liver function, hepatitis, or jaundice; occasionally rhinitis, bronchospasm, or acute pneumonia; rarely visual disturbances such as impaired vision and dark spots, hearing loss, tinnitus, or taste abnormality; fatigue, drowsiness, headache, or dizziness; occasionally anxiety, restlessness, confusion, or depression; rarely aseptic meningitis, severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, stiff neck, fever, or impaired consciousness; rarely mental abnormality, agitation, excitement, disorientation, or reversible toxic amblyopia; rarely lowered blood pressure, raised blood pressure, palpitations, oliguria, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN and blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath, or languor; rarely renal papillary necrosis, nephrotic syndrome, interstitial nephritis, peripheral edema, acute pulmonary edema, fluid retention, hypertension, heart failure, or reduced fertility in women; occasionally periorbital edema; very rarely malaise, fever, nosebleed, or worsening of inflammation.

Interactions

  • Do not take together with aspirin, other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, or high-dose methotrexate used in cancer chemotherapy (15 mg/week or more).
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if you are taking corticosteroids, alcohol, digoxin, phenytoin, probenecid, sulfinpyrazone, sulfonylureas, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists, diuretics, lithium, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), baclofen, immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, sirolimus), thrombolytics, ticlopidine, antithrombotic agents, medicines that increase blood potassium levels (trimethoprim, heparin, etc.), inducers of CYP2C8 or CYP2C9 (e.g., rifampicin, phenobarbital), low-dose methotrexate (less than 15 mg/week), antiplatelet agents, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, if you take low-dose aspirin to prevent myocardial infarction or stroke, or if you have experienced hypersensitivity or an allergic reaction to Yellow No. 5.

Those aged 15 years and older and adults take 1 bottle at a time, those aged 11 years to under 15 years take 2/3 bottle at a time, those aged 7 years to under 11 years take 1/2 bottle at a time, those aged 3 years to under 7 years take 1/3 bottle at a time, and those aged 1 year to under 3 years take 1/4 bottle at a time, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals.   • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, in patients taking acetaminophen, serious skin reactions that may be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), have been reported, and if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily amount of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take it together with other products that contain acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • Patients who are hypersensitive to this medicine, people who have experienced asthma when taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold remedies, and infants under 3 months of age and children under 2 years of age must not take this medicine.

  • When giving it to a child, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.

Interactions

  • Do not take together with other products containing acetaminophen, MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian drugs, etc.), antitussives and expectorants, other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis, motion sickness medicines, anti-allergy medicines).
  • People who stopped taking an MAO inhibitor (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian drugs, etc.) within the past 2 weeks should not take this medicine.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist if you take it together with diabetes medicines, gout medicines, arthritis medicines, anticoagulants, steroids, barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, alcohol, potassium-containing preparations, licorice-containing preparations, preparations containing glycyrrhizic acid or its salts, loop diuretics (furosemide, etacrynic acid), or thiazide diuretics (trichlormethiazide).

How it works

Why this one

Who should ask first

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 1/2 tablet to 1.5 tablets (200 to 600 mg) per dose 3 to 4 times a day, up to a maximum of 3200 mg a day. Children aged 11 to 14 years take 200 to 250 mg per dose, children aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg per dose, children aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg per dose, and children aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg per dose, orally 3 to 4 times a day. For children weighing less than 30 kg the daily amount must not exceed 500 mg, and it is preferable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. Do not take more than the recommended amount.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be taken by patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, by patients who have or have had gastrointestinal ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding, by patients with severe blood abnormality, severe liver impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency or severe high blood pressure, by patients who have or have had bronchial asthma, by patients who have or have had hypersensitivity such as asthma, urticaria or an allergic reaction to aspirin or another non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesic (including COX-2 inhibitors), by patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, by pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, by patients taking high-dose methotrexate as anticancer therapy, or by patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.

peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, hematemesis, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, thirst, stomatitis, abdominal distension, oral ulcer, constipation and black stools; mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), photosensitivity reaction, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS syndrome) of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, exfoliative dermatitis and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis; hepatitis, jaundice, hepatic dysfunction such as increases in GOT, GPT and ALP, and liver impairment; hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reaction, asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purpura, rash, itching, asthma, bronchoconstriction, difficulty breathing or wheezing; visual disturbance such as a blind area of the visual field, hearing loss, tinnitus and abnormal taste; vertigo, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness; aseptic meningitis or meningitis (symptoms such as severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever or disturbance of consciousness); and, at an unknown frequency, Conn's syndrome, periorbital swelling, facial swelling, malaise, fever, nosebleed and peripheral edema.

  • Do not take this medicine together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, low-dose aspirin, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking it together with ACE inhibitors, lithium, furosemide and thiazide diuretics, coumarin anticoagulants (such as warfarin), or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

How to take it

Adolescents aged 12 years and over and adults take 5 g once a day. It is best taken in the morning, but it may also be taken before bedtime. It may be taken with a small amount of water.

Possible side effects

  • If adverse reactions such as allergic reactions occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • While taking this medicine, do not take antipsychotics or sleeping pills.

payloads.title: Topical medicine (MFDS 198700683)
payloads.summary: This medicine is used for difficulty in expectorating sputum in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pu
payloads.content:

Topical medicine (MFDS 198700683)Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 198700683. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

This medicine is used for difficulty in expectorating sputum in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pulmonary tuberculosis, emphysema, upper respiratory tract inflammation (pharyngitis and laryngitis), lung abscess, pneumonia, cystic fibrosis and postoperative pulmonary complications, and for the preparation and aftercare of bronchography, bronchoscopy, lung cancer cytology and tracheostomy.

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Topical medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for difficulty in expectorating sputum in bronchial asthma, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pu

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 198700683. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

For nebulization therapy using a face mask, mouthpiece, or tracheostomy, nebulize 1 to 10 mL every 2 to 6 hours. The recommended amount is 3 to 5 mL nebulized 3 to 4 times a day. Nebulization therapy using a mist tent or an inhalation device (Croupette) is a method needed in special cases and is used on an individual basis according to the patient's personal needs and the convenience of the administration method. This method of administration requires a large volume of solution, and sometimes up to about 300 mL may be required for a single treatment. The recommended amount should be a volume that can maintain a very dense, fog-like state inside the tent or inhalation device throughout the treatment period. Intermittent or continuous long-term administration is desirable. For direct instillation, administer 1 to 2 mL every hour. For the routine treatment of patients who have had a tracheostomy, administer 1 to 2 mL through the tracheostomy every 1 to 4 hours. When administering directly to a specific part of the bronchial tree of the lung by inserting a small plastic catheter into the trachea under local anesthesia and a direct incision, administer 2 to 5 mL every 1 to 4 hours using a syringe connected to the catheter. For diagnostic bronchography, administer 1 to 2 mL 2 to 3 times before performing the bronchography, by nebulization or by instillation into the bronchi.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine should not use it.
  • Before using this medicine, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and breastfeeding women, patients with bronchial asthma or accompanying respiratory insufficiency, elderly people, and children should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • It is not used as an injection or as eye drops.
  • After nebulization therapy the face mask may stick to the face, but it comes off easily when washed with water.

Possible side effects

  • A mild odor (sulfur smell) may occur, sometimes bronchial obstruction, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite, and rarely anaphylaxis, bloody sputum, chills, fever, runny nose, stomatitis, drowsiness, a feeling of chest pressure, or irritation of the trachea and bronchi may occur.

Interactions

  • When it is necessary to use this medicine together with an antibiotic, inhale them separately, or give the antibiotic by injection or orally.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to use the eye drops

When needed, instill 1 to 2 drops into the affected eye. To open the container, bend the tip fully back and forth and then pull it off.

Precautions for use

  • If you swallow this medicine by mistake, get help from a doctor or another professional immediately.
  • If symptoms worsen or last for 72 hours or longer, stop using this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not reuse it after 1 use.
  • After instilling it in the eye, discard the remaining solution and the container.
  • To avoid contamination of this medicine and damage to the eye, do not let the tip of the container touch the eye or any outside surface.
  • Do not use it if the color of the solution has changed or if it has become cloudy.

Possible side effects

  • If you experience pain, changes in your field of vision, persistent redness, or irritation, stop using this medicine immediately and consult a doctor.

  • Use this medicine externally only.

  • If rash and redness, itching, swelling, irritation, a feeling of heat, scaling, desquamation (peeling of the skin like dandruff or flakes), skin maceration, dry skin and a feeling of skin tightness, or cracking of the skin occur, stop using this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Why this one

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 16 years and older may take 1 tablet (10 mg) at a time, up to 2 tablets (20 mg) a day.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or to H2 receptor antagonists, hypersensitivity to soybean oil, soybeans, or peanuts, or genetic problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if you have difficulty swallowing food or pain when swallowing, hematemesis (vomiting of blood), or bloody stools; if heartburn lasts for 3 months or longer; if dizziness or sleepiness appears together with cold sweat; if chest or shoulder pain is accompanied by shortness of breath; if chest pain occurs frequently; or if symptoms such as unexpected weight loss, nausea, vomiting, or gastrointestinal pain appear.
  • Those who have experienced hypersensitivity to medicines, patients with kidney disorder (renal impairment), heart disease, or liver disorder, elderly people, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant and nursing mothers, patients with abnormal fat metabolism such as hyperlipoproteinemia, diabetic hyperlipidemia, or pancreatitis, patients to whom lipid emulsions must be given with caution, and patients on hemodialysis should also consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If there is any change in bodily function after taking this medicine compared with before taking it, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not take this medicine for 14 days or longer.

Possible side effects

  • If shock, anaphylaxis, difficulty breathing, generalized flushing (reddening of the whole body), facial edema (swelling of the face), pharyngeal edema (swelling), urticaria, decreases in white blood cells, red blood cells, platelets, or eosinophils, anemia, delayed hemostasis, mucocutaneous ocular syndrome, epidermal necrolysis, rash, urticaria (erythema), abnormal liver function, elevation of AST (GOT) and ALT (GPT), elevation of total bilirubin and LDH, jaundice, hepatitis, muscle pain, rhabdomyolysis, joint pain, muscle cramps, bradycardia (slow pulse), tachycardia (fast pulse), chest pain, raised blood pressure, facial flushing, tinnitus (ringing in the ears), impaired consciousness, convulsions, general malaise, headache, drowsiness, insomnia, hallucinations, agitation, excitement, decreased libido, abnormal sensation, a feeling of heaviness in the head, confusion, depression, dizziness, constipation, diarrhea, thirst, nausea and vomiting, abdominal distension, loss of appetite, stomatitis (inflammation of the mouth), interstitial nephritis (inflammation of the kidney), acute renal failure, fever, abnormal kidney function test values (elevated BUN and creatinine, etc.), menstrual irregularity, interstitial pneumonia accompanied by high fever, cough, difficulty breathing and chest X-ray abnormalities, bronchospasm, gynecomastia, or taste abnormality occurs, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Before taking this medicine, patients taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, athlete's foot treatments and antifungal agents (such as itraconazole and posaconazole oral suspension), or tyrosine kinase inhibitors (dasatinib, erlotinib, gefitinib, pazopanib, etc.) should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Patients receiving intravenous lipid preparations should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking this medicine.

However, take the smallest amount for the first dose and increase or decrease the amount little by little while observing the shape and condition of the stools.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with acute abdominal conditions (appendicitis, intestinal bleeding, ulcerative colitis, etc.), patients with intestinal obstruction (blocked bowel), children aged 7 years or younger, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase (milk sugar enzyme) deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with hypersensitivity to Yellow No. 4, patients with severe abdominal pain or with nausea and vomiting, pregnant women or women who may be pregnant, people on a sodium-restricted diet, and patients with rectal bleeding or intestinal failure or those who have experienced it should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration exactly.
  • When giving it to a child, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • If there is no improvement in symptoms after about 1 week of use, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Children aged 10 years or younger should avoid taking it.
  • Do not chew the tablet when taking it.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and congested, reddened skin, itching, severe abdominal pain (stomach ache), diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, or cramps occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine within 1 hour after taking an antacid or drinking milk.

This medicine is used for the relief of the various symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore throat, cough, phlegm, chills [feeling cold and shivering], fever, headache, joint pain, muscle pain).

At a glance

Category

Over-the-counter medicine · Oral medicine

How it works

This medicine is used for the relief of the various symptoms of a cold (runny nose, nasal congestion, sneezing, sore thr

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 202105006. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Those aged 15 years and over take 1 sachet (20 mL), those aged 11 years and over but under 15 years take 2/3 of a sachet, those aged 7 years and over but under 11 years take 1/2 of a sachet, those aged 3 years and over but under 7 years take 1/3 of a sachet, and those aged 2 years and over but under 3 years take 1/4 of a sachet, 3 times a day, 30 minutes after meals. Do not administer it to children under 2 years of age. As a rule, allow an interval of 4 hours between doses.

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol every day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Very rarely, serious skin reactions that can be fatal, such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; if a skin rash or another sign of a hypersensitivity reaction appears after taking this medicine, stop taking it immediately.
  • Do not take more than the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen (4,000 mg).
  • It may cause liver damage.
  • Do not take this medicine together with other products containing acetaminophen.

Precautions for use

  • People with or with a history of hypersensitivity to this medicine, people who have had asthma after taking other antipyretic analgesics or cold medicines, infants (newborns) under 3 months of age, and people who are taking MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.) or who are within 2 weeks of stopping them must not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the following apply: an infant or young child aged 3 months and over but under 2 years; an infant or a child under 15 years of age who has, or is suspected of having, chickenpox or influenza; a person with an allergic constitution; a person who has experienced allergy to medicines (fever, rash, joint pain, asthma, itching, etc.); a person with liver, kidney, heart, or thyroid disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroduodenal ulcer, glaucoma (eye pain, blurred vision, etc.), or difficulty urinating (passing urine); an elderly person; a person in poor physical condition or a person with a high fever; a person whose gastrointestinal problems such as heartburn, stomach discomfort, or stomach pain persist or recur, or who has ulcers or bleeding problems; a pregnant woman or a woman who may be pregnant; a breastfeeding woman; or symptoms such as smoking, asthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, a cough accompanied by excessive phlegm, a cough that persists or recurs for 1 week or more, a chronic cough, or a cough accompanied by fever, rash, or a persistent headache.
  • If symptoms do not improve after taking it 5 to 6 times, consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Follow the prescribed dosage and administration carefully.
  • Do not drink alcohol while taking it.
  • Do not take it continuously for a long period.
  • When administering it to children, administer it under the guidance and supervision of a guardian.
  • Drowsiness may occur after taking it, so take care when driving or operating machinery.

Possible side effects

  • If rash and redness (congested and reddened skin), itching, nausea and vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, edema (swelling), difficulty urinating, persistent or severe thirst, dizziness, anxiety, tremor, insomnia, shock symptoms (urticaria, edema and chest tightness immediately after taking the medicine, together with pallor, cold hands and feet, cold sweat and difficulty breathing), Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome: severe symptoms accompanied by high fever, with rash and redness and blistering like a burn), asthma, generalized listlessness, jaundice (the skin or the whites of the eyes turning yellow), or interstitial pneumonia (accompanied by coughing, breathlessness, difficulty breathing, fever, etc.) occur, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Interactions

  • Do not take this medicine together with MAO inhibitors (antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood regulators, antiparkinsonian agents, etc.), antitussive-expectorants (cough and phlegm remedies), other cold remedies, antipyretic analgesics, sedatives, or oral medicines containing antihistamines (oral preparations for rhinitis [nasal inflammation], motion sickness remedies, anti-allergy remedies).
  • Patients who have taken barbiturates, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol should consult a doctor or pharmacist.

How to apply it

Before application, wash the affected area (the diseased area) clean, dry it completely, and then spray an appropriate amount once a day.

Precautions for use

  • This medicine must not be used by patients who have or have had hypersensitivity to this medicine, by a pregnant woman or a woman who may be pregnant or a breast-feeding woman, or by young children and children, and it must not be used on the eyes or around the eyes, on mucous membranes (the mouth, the nose, the vagina, etc.), on the scrotum or the external genitals, on an affected area (a diseased part) with severe eczema, moistness, erosion or wounds, on the nails or on the scalp.
  • Before using this medicine, consult a doctor or pharmacist if the user has an allergic constitution, if the affected area (the diseased part) is on the face or is extensive or has suppuration, or if it is unclear whether the condition is "eczema" or "athlete's foot, tinea cruris (ringworm of the groin) or tinea corporis".
  • Follow the prescribed directions and amounts.
  • Do not use it while the affected area (the diseased part) or its surroundings are contaminated.
  • Be careful to keep it out of the eyes, and if it does get into the eyes, rinse them immediately with water or lukewarm water.
  • Use it externally only and do not use it internally.
  • Shake it well before use.
  • Spray it from a distance of 5 cm from the affected area (the diseased part), and check the nozzle carefully so that it is not sprayed toward or inhaled into the face, especially the eyes.
  • Because of the risk of frostbite and similar injury, do not spray it on the same area continuously for 1 second or more.
  • Do not let the eyes or mucous membranes be touched by hands on which this medicine has been left.
  • If the symptoms do not get better after about 2 weeks of use, or if the symptoms worsen because of the use of this medicine, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Possible side effects

  • If skin rash, redness (reddening from congestion), lacquer-type dermatitis, itching, swelling (puffiness), a feeling of irritation, a feeling of heat, peeling of the skin (flaking), erosion (maceration), dryness or cracking of the skin (splitting) occurs, stop using it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not use this medicine together with hydrogen peroxide.

Category

How it works

Why this one

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to take it

Adults take 1 capsule per dose, 1 time a day. Since this medicine is an enteric-coated capsule, it may be taken before meals with plenty of water.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine or other salicylate preparations, patients with peptic ulcer, patients with aspirin-induced asthma (induction of asthma attacks by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, etc.) or those who have experienced it, patients with hemophilia, severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, or a bleeding tendency, patients receiving concomitant methotrexate at a dose of 15 milligrams or more per week (15 mg/week), and pregnant women in the third trimester of pregnancy should not take this medicine.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with renal impairment, cardiovascular circulatory dysfunction, hepatic impairment, cardiac dysfunction, blood abnormalities, or bronchial asthma, patients about to undergo surgery, infants aged 3 years or younger, patients who have experienced hypersensitivity to analgesics, anti-inflammatory drugs, or antirheumatic drugs or other allergic diseases, elderly people, patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, and patients with hypersensitivity to Yellow No. 5 should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Take care not to damage the enteric coating of this medicine.
  • If you are to undergo surgery (including dental surgery), you must tell the doctor in charge that you are taking an aspirin preparation and receive advice.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms (for example, difficulty breathing, generalized flushing, angioedema, urticaria), asthma attacks, erythema, itching, nasal congestion, cardiac and respiratory disorders, occasionally rash, swelling, urticaria, rhinitis symptoms, conjunctivitis, rarely toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), mucocutaneous ocular syndrome (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), exfoliative dermatitis, rarely aplastic anemia, anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function (prolonged bleeding time), ringing in the ears, hearing loss, dizziness, headache, agitation, rarely liver disorder, very rarely temporary liver damage with elevated liver transaminases, kidney disorder, acute renal failure, hyperventilation, metabolic acidosis, excessive drop in body temperature, collapse, or coldness of the limbs occur, stop taking this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Loss of appetite, heartburn, stomach pain, nausea, and vomiting may occur.

Interactions

  • Do not use it together with other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesics, salicylate preparations, or high-dose methotrexate.
  • Consult a doctor or pharmacist when taking it together with anticoagulants, thrombolytics or other platelet aggregation inhibitors, hemostatics, antidiabetic medicines (insulin preparations, tolbutamide, etc.), uricosuric agents (benzbromarone, probenecid), lithium preparations, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, digoxin, systemically acting adrenocortical hormone preparations (except hydrocortisone used as replacement therapy for Addison's disease), angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, valproic acid, or alkaline preparations (e.g. sodium bicarbonate, magnesium carbonate).

  • If dermatitis, a foul odor of sweat and breath, hair loss, restlessness, vomiting, or allergy occurs, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

  • Do not take reducing agents such as vitamin C together with this medicine.

How to take it

For rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, soft tissue injury, non-articular rheumatic disease, acute gout, and psoriatic arthritis, adults take 200-600 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. Up to a maximum of 3,200 mg a day may be taken. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, take 30 to 40 mg per kg of body weight per dose, in 3 to 4 divided doses a day. For mild to moderate pain and for colds, adults take 200 to 400 mg per dose, 3 to 4 times a day. The dose may be increased or decreased as appropriate according to age and symptoms. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years take 200 to 250 mg (10 to 12.5 mL) per dose, those aged 7 to 10 years take 150 to 200 mg (7.5 to 10 mL) per dose, those aged 3 to 6 years take 100 to 150 mg (5 to 7.5 mL) per dose, and those aged 1 to 2 years take 50 to 100 mg (2.5 to 5 mL) per dose, 3 to 4 times a day, and it is advisable to avoid taking it on an empty stomach. For children, those aged 11 to 14 years may take up to 1,000 mg (50 mL) a day, those aged 7 to 10 years up to 800 mg (40 mL), those aged 3 to 6 years up to 600 mg (30 mL), and those aged 1 to 2 years up to 400 mg (20 mL).

Warning

  • People who regularly drink three or more glasses of alcohol a day should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine or another antipyretic analgesic.
  • It may cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Taking this medicine increases the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic reactions, myocardial infarction and stroke, which may be fatal, and serious gastrointestinal adverse reactions such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcer and perforation may appear.
  • Patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure, congestive heart failure, established ischemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease or cerebrovascular disease must avoid taking high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day), and patients who have cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, smoking, etc.) and need to take high-dose ibuprofen (2,400 mg a day) should consult a doctor or pharmacist before taking this medicine.

Precautions for use

  • Patients with hypersensitivity to this medicine, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, severe blood abnormalities, severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment, severe cardiac insufficiency, severe high blood pressure, or bronchial asthma, patients who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions caused by aspirin or other anti-inflammatory analgesics, patients with pain occurring before or after coronary artery bypass surgery, pregnant women in the last 3 months of pregnancy, breastfeeding women, patients receiving high-dose methotrexate as cancer chemotherapy, and patients with hereditary problems such as galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency, or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.
  • Do not take more than the recommended dose.
  • Before taking this medicine, patients with blood abnormalities or a bleeding tendency, patients with liver cirrhosis, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, cardiac insufficiency, heart disease, high blood pressure, systemic lupus erythematosus, mixed connective tissue disease, ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease, elderly people, children under 2 years of age, pregnant women, and patients with chickenpox should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • When taking it for a cold, take it for no more than 5 days as a rule, and without the direction of a doctor or pharmacist do not take it for pain for 10 days or more (adults) or 5 days or more (children), and do not take it for fever for 3 days or more.

  • If shock (difficulty breathing, fall in blood pressure, etc.), blood disorders such as decreased hematocrit, decreased hemoglobin, anemia, aplastic anemia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, granulocytopenia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, reduced platelet function or eosinophilia, peptic ulcer, gastrointestinal ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation, ulcerative colitis, bloody stools, gastritis, pancreatitis, vomiting of blood, Crohn's disease, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, indigestion, diarrhea, stomach discomfort, upper abdominal pain, dry mouth, stomatitis, abdominal distension, oral ulcers, constipation, black stools, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis (Lyell's syndrome), drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms of unknown frequency, angioneurotic edema, bullous dermatitis, erythema multiforme, maculopapular rash, reddening of the skin, blisters, rash, exfoliative dermatitis, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, hepatitis, jaundice, abnormal liver function, liver disorder, hypersensitivity or anaphylactic reaction, asthma attack, urticaria, eczema, purple spots, visual disturbance, deafness, ringing in the ears, taste abnormality, vertigo, drowsiness, dizziness, depression, headache, cerebrovascular accident or nervousness, aseptic meningitis or meningitis (severe headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, a stiff neck, fever or impaired consciousness), acute renal failure, decreased urination, hematuria, proteinuria, elevated BUN or blood creatinine, hyperkalemia, interstitial nephritis, nephrotic syndrome, renal papillary necrosis, decreased urine volume, generalized edema and the accompanying shortness of breath or listlessness, Kounis syndrome of unknown frequency, swelling around the eyes, facial swelling, malaise, fever, nosebleed, swelling or peripheral edema appear, stop taking it immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

How it works

This medicine is used for disinfection of the patient's skin before surgery or before insertion of a syringe needle or a

Why this one

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 201801818. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

Use this medicine in the following order. Remove the applicator from its packaging and hold it with the sponge facing downwards. Do not touch the sponge part of the applicator. Squeeze the applicator firmly only once so that the ampoule breaks and the solution comes out, and leave the broken ampoule inside the applicator. For the 26 mL product, squeeze the lever on the handle firmly, and for the other products squeeze both wings firmly. Do not squeeze or press the wings repeatedly in order to wet the sponge quickly. Press and release the sponge against the treatment area until the solution is visible on the skin, wetting the sponge and completely wetting the treatment area with the solution. For a dry surgical site (e.g. the abdomen or an arm), once the solution is visible on the skin, rub gently back and forth for 30 seconds to treat that area. For a moist surgical site (e.g. the groin fold), rub gently back and forth repeatedly for about 2 minutes. Let the area to which the solution has been applied dry completely in the air, and do not wipe the solution off. Discard the applicator after a single use, together with any remaining solution that was not used on the treatment area. It is not necessary to use the entire amount.

Precautions for use

  • People with hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine, isopropanol, or Yellow No. 5 and infants aged 2 months or younger should not use this medicine.
  • Do not use this medicine for disinfecting surgical instruments, or on nervous tissue (e.g., brain or spinal cord tissue), the eyes, ears, mouth, mucous membranes, genital mucous membranes, open wounds, or torn or damaged skin, or for general washing of the skin.
  • Before using this medicine, people with hypersensitivity to other medicines, people who have experienced allergic diseases such as asthma or who have a family history of them, people with hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine preparations, and people with a drug-hypersensitive constitution should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Use it externally only on intact skin.
  • Contact with the eyes may cause corneal damage, so be careful not to let it get into the eyes; if it does get in, rinse thoroughly with clean water immediately.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms (nausea, malaise, cold sweat, dizziness, a stifling feeling, difficulty breathing, redness, a sudden drop in blood pressure, urticaria, angioedema, etc.), occasionally rash, photosensitization, irritation, sensitization, erythema or inflammation, itching, dry and thinly peeling skin, local pain at the application site, or local skin reactions, or very rarely rash (e.g., erythematous, papular, or maculopapular), blisters, small blisters at the application site, a burning sensation of the skin, dermatitis, eczema, chemical burns in newborns, eye irritation, congestion, impaired vision, or eye damage occurs, stop using this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Who should ask first

If any item in the safety information applies to you, ask the pharmacist at the store first.

How to apply it

Use this medicine in the following order. Remove the applicator from its packaging and hold it with the sponge facing downwards. Do not touch the sponge part of the applicator. Squeeze the applicator firmly only once so that the ampoule breaks and the solution comes out, and leave the broken ampoule inside the applicator. For the 26 mL product, squeeze the lever on the handle firmly, and for the other products squeeze both wings firmly. Do not squeeze or press the wings repeatedly in order to wet the sponge quickly. Press and release the sponge against the treatment area until the solution is visible on the skin, wetting the sponge and completely wetting the treatment area with the solution. For a dry surgical site (e.g. the abdomen or an arm), once the solution is visible on the skin, rub gently back and forth for 30 seconds to treat that area. For a moist surgical site (e.g. the groin fold), rub gently back and forth repeatedly for about 2 minutes. Let the area to which the solution has been applied dry completely in the air, and do not wipe the solution off. Discard the applicator after a single use, together with any remaining solution that was not used on the treatment area. It is not necessary to use the entire amount.

Precautions for use

  • People with hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine, isopropanol, or Yellow No. 5 and infants aged 2 months or younger should not use this medicine.
  • Do not use this medicine for disinfecting surgical instruments, or on nervous tissue (e.g., brain or spinal cord tissue), the eyes, ears, mouth, mucous membranes, genital mucous membranes, open wounds, or torn or damaged skin, or for general washing of the skin.
  • Before using this medicine, people with hypersensitivity to other medicines, people who have experienced allergic diseases such as asthma or who have a family history of them, people with hypersensitivity to chlorhexidine preparations, and people with a drug-hypersensitive constitution should consult a doctor or pharmacist.
  • Use it externally only on intact skin.
  • Contact with the eyes may cause corneal damage, so be careful not to let it get into the eyes; if it does get in, rinse thoroughly with clean water immediately.

Possible side effects

  • If shock symptoms (nausea, malaise, cold sweat, dizziness, a stifling feeling, difficulty breathing, redness, a sudden drop in blood pressure, urticaria, angioedema, etc.), occasionally rash, photosensitization, irritation, sensitization, erythema or inflammation, itching, dry and thinly peeling skin, local pain at the application site, or local skin reactions, or very rarely rash (e.g., erythematous, papular, or maculopapular), blisters, small blisters at the application site, a burning sensation of the skin, dermatitis, eczema, chemical burns in newborns, eye irritation, congestion, impaired vision, or eye damage occurs, stop using this medicine immediately and consult a doctor or pharmacist.

Based on the official MFDS approval for product code 200101057. Check the ingredient and strength rather than the product name.
